One former Rockstar Games lead has a revolutionary take about GTA 6 – "it is good." But even though that may be the case, he reckons that "the complaints are real" in Chapter 1 from those suggesting that it "doesn't feel like a sandbox" and instead feels like a "girlfriend simulator."

Obbe Vermeij worked at Rockstar Games between 1995 and 2009, serving as technical director on GTA 3, 4, Vice City, and San Andreas. Obviously, he'd left the studio well before GTA 6 started development (it might have been a long time coming, but it wasn't that long), so he's been playing through it alongside the rest of us.

"It is good. Very good," he begins in a post on Twitter. However, there's a "but" coming.

"In chapter 1 (The first 8 hours or so) the game doesn't give you much choice," he continues. "There are many tutorials, cut scenes, mandatory missions and the missions are basic. The complaints are real (realism over gameplay, girlfriend simulator, doesn't feel like a sandbox)."

Opinions here do vary – I've definitely seen more than a few social media posts complaining about the optional tasks of grocery shopping for Lucia and buying her flowers, for example. They probably weren't high up the list of activities fans who planned to enter Leonida and immediately commit heinous crimes had in mind, I suppose – though it's worth keeping in mind that, again, those parts are optional.

Equally, though, I've seen plenty of people enjoying the almost life-sim-esque vibe of GTA 6's opening hours, and that's probably reflected in how much time people spend in that first chapter. As someone who spent 18 hours in Chapter 1, you can probably guess what camp I fall into.

Regardless, though, Vermeij reckons things really pick up by the time you reach the second chapter. "In chapter 2, the game backs off and gives you a bunch of missions to choose from," he says. "This is when the GTA magic kicks in."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Vermeij says he's now 46% of the way through the story in Chapter 3 and "having loads of fun now." He concludes that the "production values are unreal," and I don't think anyone could disagree with that.

GTA 6 reviews have been glowing across the board, and Rockstar has already achieved almost unfathomable commercial success, with a whopping 32.5 million copies sold via pre-orders (eclipsing a figure that took Elden Ring three years to reach) and earning $3.79 billion on day one. It had the biggest entertainment launch in history – I don't think the devs could have hoped for anything better.

#3821. The Game Awards just confirmed who plays GTA 6's Lucia

Manni L. Perez has been confirmed as the actress behind Grand Theft Auto 6's Lucia Caminos, just days before the game launches.

As spotted by IGN, the confirmation came during The Game Awards' nominations livestream today, where Perez was nominated for Best Performance for her role as co-lead Lucia.

Perez had been widely rumoured to play Lucia for months, and fans have regularly filled her social media livestreams with questions about GTA 6, which she has been oh-so-carefully sidestepping.

Lucia is one half of GTA 6's lead pair alongside Jason Duval, making it the first Grand Theft Auto game with a playable couple.

Jason's actor wasn't among the nominees, so who plays him is still a mystery.

Perez has previously had guest roles in a string of US TV dramas, including Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Chicago P.D., The Blacklist, and Blindspot, and has also done voice work for GTA Online.

Funnily enough, Lucia isn't her first Lucia - she also played Lucia Santiago in a 2023 episode of CBS's East New York.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

It's long been revealed that GTA 6 will have a regional release, meaning that some lucky, soon-to-be players will be able to access the game much earlier than others. Rockstar's regional release schedule sees the game launching at midnight on 19th November regardless of what region you're in, and if you wish to join those playing almost a day early, there's the good ol' Xbox New Zealand trick for eager players to try.

#3820. Worst Class Ever takes asymmetrical multiplayer back to school, with a teacher player trying to spot the naughty children among the NPCs

Master the sinful art of eating sweets behind your textbook

What's the best prank you ever pulled on a teacher in school, assuming you went to school? By which I mean, a genuinely funny prank that didn't cause any injuries, break any of the more important laws (legal or ethical), or leave anybody with years of mental distress.

I'll start: I once had to write a four-page punishment essay with the topic "silence is golden", after being caught talking in class. I took the essay very seriously for the first three pages, only to end it with the phrase "...but not as golden as my arse." The teacher who set me the essay smugly tore it up without reading it - as I knew he would. Checkmate, Mr Thompson. Decades later, the last laugh remains mine.

Worst Class Ever is a new don't-call-it-friendslop asymmetrical multiplayer game dedicated to such larks. One player is a teacher, and seven others are naughty delinquent children, hiding in amongst some well-brought-up and obedient NPCs. As the wayward tykes, your goal is to do mischievous things like eating at your desk, passing notes, dropping banana skins, and playing on your phone, without being spotted by Teach.

All of this takes place in a breezy modern Japanese high school, the kind familiar from a million animes. Bagsy the Protagonist Desk by the window at the back of the class! The maplist spans the curriculum, from computer labs to gym tracks to stepped lecture theatres. I don't think there are any covert edu-tainment mechanics, but if you're playing Teacher, I guess there's nothing to stop you actually explaining the periodic table while trying to work out who keeps throwing chalk at your head.

What a wholesome and whimsical place! Such happy memories! Oh crikey, the male teacher is terrifying – why can't he stop grinning? And why do I have a smoke grenade? Why is this lesson taking place in the dark? Why are the teachers permitted to punch the students and tie them to wooden posts? Worst Class Ever definitely isn't a horror game, but I'm not sure I'd send my kids to this particular institution. I feel like we're one texture pack away from playing a more sociable version of Little Nightmares. Read more on Steam.

Deciding whether to proceed or postpone the Protective Custody story mission is a big choice you'll need to make in GTA 6. The mission appears on your map as "Meet Abe" in Chapter 5, once you've completed the mission Operation Savage Glory.

Once you get to Abe's office, Jason will warn Lucia that everything will change after this mission. Lucia will hesitate at the door as you make your choice to "Proceed" or "Postpone."

This is a pretty big decision, because Protective Custody kicks off the final mission of the game which takes about an hour to play. And even though it's a binary choice between "Proceed" (which starts the mission) and "Postpone" (which delays the mission)" there's actually a third possible outcome based on when you make the choice.

It's a long mission that will take about an hour to play, so be prepared. You can't save during this mission so make sure you've got the time! Once you've completed the final mission, you can watch the credits and return to the open world so you can continue playing.

You will go back to the open world to continue playing. The "Meet Abe" icon will remain on your map so you can begin the final mission at any point from then on.

There are multiple endings to GTA 6, and I won't spoil them here. But one of the endings is only possible if you postpone the Protective Custody mission until you've deposited $2 million into your Buck Me savings account. That's why when you choose to proceed with the final mission makes a difference.

It's also worth noting (again, without spoilers) that just because you do have $2 million in your Buck Me savings account does not guarantee you will see this particular ending. There are still choices you'll need to make in the final mission that determine which ending you see.

Original Story: Rockstar Games has today published the first GTA 6 post-launch update on PS5, bringing its open worlder up to version number 01.002.002.

#3817. Firaxis reportedly cuts a third of its staff as studio head departs and new XCOM struggles

UPDATE: A WARN notice filed in Maryland confirms 37 layoffs.

Update 22nd November: A WARN notice filed in Maryland, where Firaxis is headquartered, shows that 37 employees based at the studio's Hunt Valley office have been laid off.

As noted by Vertical Slice, it's not clear whether that figure accounts for everyone affected, as Bloomberg has previously reported that around 60 people had lost their jobs.

The cuts, which took place today, account for about a third of the studio’s staff, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. Studio head Heather Hazen is also leaving.

Its sources say Firaxis' unannounced XCOM game has faced development struggles and missed "a significant milestone over the summer". The project will continue, but "may face a shakeup as a result of the cuts".

A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two label that runs Firaxis, confirmed Hazen's departure to Bloomberg, and said the studio is "restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years".

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis," the spokesperson continued. "These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."

The layoffs come two days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, which is developed and published by Rockstar, a separate label at Take-Two.

In September, around 18 months after Civ 7's widely criticised launch - and as the legendary 4X series celebrates its 35th anniversary - Firaxis unveiled a host of new updates coming to the game as it continued to improve it. These included an atomic age update, dragging Civ 7 into the present and beyond, as well as its first paid expansion, Earthrise, both arriving next year.

Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick admitted earlier this year that the studio "got it wrong with Civ 7".

"The game is a really good game. And it's certainly a profitable enterprise for us. But this is one where I think what we tried to do was a bridge too far, from the consumer's perspective," he told Game File in May.

It’s not the first round of cuts at the studio - 2K confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs at Firaxis in September 2025, and around 30 jobs went in 2023.

#3815. While soulslikes went bigger than big, Death's Door swung open the appeal of a tighter adventure

Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones. Elden Rings and Silksongs, with vast kingdoms and deep, rattling toolkits for surviving them. The reason it’s a fool’s game is because you can also have something like Death’s Door, a taut, compact, lighthearted little actioner that fills eight hours instead of 80 and yet never feels underwhelming or compromised for it.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition. You are a crow. You hit things. Occasionally you shoot things. You collect the souls of a frog, a yeti, and a grandmother. Everything in-between directly relates to finding the errant monster/pensioner, or at a stretch, upgrading one of those four abilities.

Still, it’s clever with its limitations. Environments are small in number but vary wildly in tone and texture, and they tightly weave their paths into criss-crossing bundles that maximise travel – evoking the sense of a great, ranging adventure within relatively tiny spaces. The lack of a wiki’s worth of combat options also never becomes a problem, partly because it spreads out its spell unlocks, and partly because the smooth, flowing back-and-forths of its central swordplay are pleasurable enough to carry it anyway. Good bosses, too! They’re all characterful, memorable weirdoes who fight unlike anyone in their minion armies, and usually come with a hidden weakness to deduce and exploit.

Which is welcome, as these big lads and lasses do tend to launch difficulty spikes right up your feathered backside, and do so in a game that isn’t otherwise as fussed about trial-and-error pain endurance as some of its inspirations. They don’t, however, bring the mood down. At times, this tale of a pitch-black soul reaper working as an agent of Death (complete with an office of Death and embittered co-workers of Death) can get downright cosy, leading through you through warmly-lit jungles and breezy waterside ruins.

Recently replaying, I’d also forgotten how witty it can be. Little gaglets are sprinkled throughout, both visual and verbal, but the best jokes are saved for – funnily enough – the bosses, who’ll raise your pre-fight spirit with some amusingly terrible trash talk before becoming the punchline themselves. I audibly wheezed the first time a death animation immediately cut to the foe’s impromptu funeral, their beaked killer among the precious few guests. And even when the joke is recycled later, I couldn’t help tittering at the sight of my enemy – who seconds earlier, had been attempting to fatally sit on me – lying nobly in state.

I previously considered ending my Valor Mortis review by calling it a gateway into the more demanding side of action-RPGs; a shorter, simpler alternative to FromSoft’s overwhelming titans that might nonetheless serve to introduce curious newcomers to their shared quirks and qualities. The game equivalent of splashing your chest with water before jumping into a pool. In hindsight, Death’s Door was always a better fit for that description, though there’s enough else here you don’t need to be prepping for something tougher to appreciate its lean, keen adventuring.

#3814. The Game Awards 2026 nominees announced, and GTA 6 leads with eight nods before it's even out

The Game Awards 2026 nominees have been revealed, and Grand Theft Auto 6 leads the pack with eight nominations, two days before it even launches.

Rockstar's crime epic is up for Game of the Year, Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Audio Design, and Best Action/Adventure Game. Its eighth nomination is Manni L. Perez's Best Performance nod for her role as Lucia, which is how we found out who plays her in the first place.

THE GAME AWARDS: 2026 Nominee Reveal! (Game of the Year) THE GAME AWARDS: 2026 Nominee Reveal!Watch on YouTube

For Game of the Year, GTA 6 is up against 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Nintendo is the most-nominated publisher, with 12 nominations across its games, followed by Capcom with 11, and Annapurna Interactive and PlayStation with nine each.

The nominees were picked by a jury of more than 160 media and creator outlets, who may get advance or pre-release access to games - which explains how GTA 6 made the cut before launch. The winners will be revealed on Thursday, 10th December, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Fans can vote on The Game Awards' website until 6pm PT on 9th December.

This year's show will stream for free on more than 40 platforms, including YouTube, Twitch, Prime Video, and Steam. Last year's show drew an estimated 171 million livestreams, up 11 percent on 2024's 154 million.

Use of generative AI in game dev remains as contentious as it does ubiquitous—a recent GDC report found that around 40% of devs use AI, but more than half think its influence has been negative. Ubisoft is continuing to double down on the technology, this time with Motherbrain, a new subsidiary fashioned from the team behind its "first playable generative AI experience."

As reported by VGC, Motherbrain's purpose is to develop "AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences … Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large scale systemic worlds," according to an earnings report which was released Thursday.

The information comes at a turbulent time for the publishing giant, which just laid off 166 employees even after Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced "outperformed expectations." A sweeping internal overhaul earlier this year saw the company reorganize its workforce into a throng of "creative houses," a decision which led to swathes of layoffs and six project cancellations, including the Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time Remake.

It's not clear what Motherbrain are at work on, in specific terms, right now, but there may be some clues in its past work. That playable AI "experience" I mentioned earlier is none other than Teammates, an R&D project based on a prior experiment with uncanny AI "neo-NPCs."

Teammates aimed to allow players to command NPC squadmates in a rudimentary shooter game with a microphone, and using AI, have those squadmates react believably. It's not far off, at least conceptually, from what we've seen in games like Where Winds Meet and Fortnite, both of which have experimented with AI-powered NPCs.

#3812. Former GTA 4 and Red Dead boss thinks "we are one Toy Story moment away" from people accepting gen-AI in game development in the West

"In the East, they've already accepted it."

Ben Feder, the former Take-Two CEO who oversaw the launch of massive hits like Grand Theft Auto 4, Red Dead Redemption, Borderlands, and BioShock during his tenure, believes the resistance against gen-AI in games will vanish once the games industry has its 'Toy Story moment'.

"When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance," Feder told The Game Business. "People didn't think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it."

Feder argued that the success of Toy Story ended the resistance against computer-generated animation, and the same could happen to games. Feder added, "My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in video games in the West. In the East, they've already accepted it."

Feder, who currently heads up venture capital fund Tirta Ventures, is investing in AI-first games. He, however, doesn't necessarily believe AI will reduce development costs, but that it also offers other advantages that could help game makers keep up with shifting consumer tastes.

"A lot of incumbents think about AI as a way of reducing costs, which it is," Feder said. "I query whether it will actually reduce costs, or will it just make games bigger for the same cost? But we're more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay."

Feder views gen-AI simply as new technology that allows developers to do things they couldn't before. He likened it to Unreal Engine's instancing technology, which allowed Fortnite and other battle royale games to support 100+ players in a single server.

"That's question number one as we think about what we invest in: Was this possible before AI?" Feder said of his VC firm's strategy. "And when AI gets better, does the game get better? That's harder for an incumbent to focus on, because they deploy a lot of capital, have enormous advantages in terms of distribution, capital, and IP, and all of that needs to be protected."

There's been enormous pushback from players, developers and pundits against the use of gen-AI in games. Even so, more and more studios have revealed using some gen-AI during development, such as to assist with coding. More broadly, gen-AI adoption is on the rise across the industry, with a recent report estimating 40 percent of developers are using it.

Some development studios, such as Fortnite maker Epic Games, have doubled down on the use of gen-AI in game development. Epic is even more bullish on gen-AI in its Unreal Engine, which the company is currently transforming into an engine that's almost entirely driven by gen-AI and LLMs. Consumer sentiment remains sour, however, and the perception of the tool is not helped by the number of 'AI slop' games taking over Steam's storefront, the 'enshittification' of fan wikis, or the link AI seems to have to the unprecedented wave of layoffs that has shaken the industry over the past two years.

#3811. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is getting three big updates with new starting scenarios - organ trading, junk empires and fine dining

Mucky and disreputable kiosk game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim is getting three big updates over the next few months that add extra starting scenarios, building on the existing wealth of goods, materials, vocations and techs. Those starting scenarios range from peddling human meat to running the finest cyber-frappucino stall this side of Tannhäuser Gate. There are no hard release dates, and the contents of each update may alter, but developers Questing Goose Studio have shared some rough timeframes.

Coming up in mid-December, there's the Junker starting scenario, which I assume is all about trading scrap, rather than being a Prussian nobleman. You'll get a bespoke perk, new items, and the ability to hire, equip and send scavs on expeditions. This update will also include some minor expansions for the Fence and Gunsmith vocations – the latter will be able to flog or otherwise make use of shotgun shells, 25mm grenade rounds and a tier 3 handmade SMG, alongside new armour.

Late January is when you'll "very likely" get the chance to be an Organ Dealer, care of the second major update. "Players will start by buying different organs and fulfilling specific requests, and will later be able to grow or print organs," a Steam blog explains. You'll also be able to filter blood and remove diseases, with different blood types having different value modifiers. How will you get your hands on organs? By sending horrible black market thugs on foraging "expeditions".

Last but not least, the planned April update will add the Street Food Vendor starting scenario. This lets you weave a livelihood around choice beverages and edibles from a range of cultures, supported by updates to the game's Aquaculture and Hydroponics tech. Sounds a lot cheerier than the organ trading racket, but then again, Probably Stolen will doubtless find a way to make it utterly grim. Guests at Sweeney's Cantina know better than to ask what our frappucinos are made of.

Are you playing Probably Stolen? It's been doing better than expected. I was keen on the demo, but my attention was lured away by a truly upsetting game about dogpeople in caves.

#3809. Blade director reflects on scrapped Marvel movie, says "life's too short to make sh*t films"

Bassam Tariq gets candid on his Blade experience

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The director of Marvel's scrapped Blade movie, Bassam Tariq, has reflected candidly on his time working on the movie.

The film was set to star Mahershala Ali as the titular vampire hunter, but it never actually made its way to screens.

"It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script. You're sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you," he told The New Arab, when asked what his time in the studio system taught him.

"That's also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn't add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot," he continued. "All I have is my integrity, and I've been thinking about that a lot.

"If you're the bearer of bad news to your actors, but you're not the one making any of these decisions – and it's actually coming from a corporate entity – that's not a great way to be a director," he shared. "I know some people can take that and run with it, but I learned I was losing credibility with my actors, and it wasn't a healthy way to operate as a filmmaker."

Then, Tariq got even franker about the experience. "Life's too short to make shit films, so that was my big lesson: I have to have full control over my script," he said. "If we disagree, it's between them and me. It's quite sad because we had such high hopes for what we wanted to build."

However, he added that he was pleased Ryan Coogler's Sinners was able to make use of Ruth E. Carter's costumes, because that film "feels so much bolder than what we could have accomplished."

Ali has also been very upfront about his thoughts on the movie failing to materialize. "That's a Kevin Feige question," he said when asked why the film didn't happen. "They had, as you said, a two-time Oscar winning actor under contract, and you got billions of dollars. That's a question for them, why it didn't happen. I don't mean anything personal to you, but I don't know why it did. To this day, I don't know why it didn't happen. I just know that Kevin said it was the biggest failure of his career, and I agree."

Next up for Marvel is Avengers: Doomsday, which brings together a supersized cast that includes Chris Hemsworth's Thor, Anthony Mackie's Captain America, the Fantastic Four, the Thunderbolts, and more.

Doomsday arrives this December 18. While you wait, check out our guide to all the upcoming Marvel movies and TV shows for everything else that's on the way.

#3807. Blizzard suspends World of Warcraft: Forever gold exploit abusers, puts trading blocks on their accounts and removes ill-gotten funds for good measure

Players who abused World of Warcraft: Forever's Blackmaw Hold unintended gold farm, which allowed a small minority of players to hoard thousands of gold in a few days, have drawn the ire of WoW publisher, Blizzard. Suspensions have been issued, trade locks have been put on accounts, and ill-gotten gold is being seized.

For those unaware, the World of Warcraft: Forever community was greatly alarmed by this gold farm, which had players clear the same non-elite enemies from the new late game dungeon, Blackmaw Hold. By quickly clearing select mobs with area-of-effect damage, players would loot upwards of 100 raw gold an hour. This exploit, clearly not intentional, was nonetheless farmed until Blizzard hotfixed it earlier in the week.

There was much speculation on what would happen to those who participated in this exploit. That speculation would come to an end late last night with an official statement from the World of Warcraft: Forever development team.

"As players continue their journey into WoW Forever’s higher-level content, we are closely monitoring the game economy to ensure that gold sources and costs are well balanced," the statement reads. "Finding efficient farming spots has always been part of the game, and is how most players have earned their epic mounts since 2004. When a single location proves so lucrative that it overshadows all other sources, we generally adjust it to bring it in line with the rest."

It goes on to explain the nature of the bug that made this gold farm possible, before reassuring those who may have accidentally benefited from some extra cash from their regular runs of Blackmaw Hold they have nothing to worry about. The same cannot be said for those who took advantage of the situation.

"Players who simply ran Blackmaw Hold a few times and benefited organically from the extra loot did nothing wrong, and no one should worry that they’re putting their account at risk if they accidentally benefit from a bug," it continues. "But there were a couple hundred players worldwide who recognized that this was unintended and spent significant time exclusively farming that group of enemies.

"Yesterday, we put an economy lock on their accounts to prevent broader impact to the game economy while we investigated the extent of the exploitative gains, including gold earned by vendoring bugged drops. Today, we are in the process of removing all such gold earned, as well as applying account suspensions to significant abusers."

The post concludes by thanking players for their feedback on the matter, and a final warning: "As always, we advise all players to refrain from abusing game mechanics that are clearly unintended. We will continue to take action against intentional abuse."

This decision certainly sets the precedent moving forward with World of Warcraft: Forever that such exploits won't be tolerated, and rolling back the wealth of those who made out of Blackmaw Hold like bandits is a good measure that should prevent continuous damage.

Inevitably the exploit would have had some impact, specifically in those days prior to trading blocks being put in place. While the gold on the exploiter's accounts may be removed, any purchases they made on the in-game auction house will have affected others through buying and selling goods with ample funds.

Those who were suspended temporarily will be able to regain access to the game by the time the first wave of raids come out in December, so it very much feels like a firm slap on the wrist in that regard. Even so, given the establishment of punishments for such behavior, one can only wonder if future events will come with harsher penalties.

World of Warcraft: Forever, despite this small economic roadbump, is proving exceptionally popular for Blizzard. It's already broken records for the series, and has impressed players so far with its revamping of the classic MMO.

If you were waiting for Black Friday to upgrade your Xbox gaming experience, then you'll be pretty glad to know that you don't need to wait at all. Not all retailers have begun their discounts yet, but some have, and some top picks have already been brought down to their lowest-ever prices.

Early Black Friday sales at Walmart have come to a selection of gaming tech, including many kinds of Xbox accessory. Most of these deals are on controllers and headsets, the two most common kind of peripheral sold for Microsoft's console, but I've found some useful other items reduced too. The deals you'll find below are all from brands we trust, and many of the discounts beat what other retailers are offering right now too.

Not only does Walmart seem to be one of the few brands with an early Black Friday deal on this advanced Xbox controller, but it's reduced $20 further than it's gone in the past. The catch? Only the white model is discounted/

Don't need the top-end Xbox controller? Several colors of the standard model are also reduced, for if you've broken your first or want some couch gameplay. This isn't a new low price for the controller, but it's the usual discount price, and we don't always see as many colorways reduced.

Happy with a wired Xbox controller? We praised the G7 SE as a solid budget pick, and now it's 45% off. The black model is slightly cheaper than the rest, enough that it beats a similar discount on the G7 SE on Amazon.

If you want to modify how your controller feels, for more competitive responses or just comfort, then thumb grips can really help. GameSir is a reliable maker of them, and several color packs are discounted; black is the cheapest at nearly half off.

We haven't tested this headset, but I've enjoyed previous Quantum sets as good-value gaming cans. At half price, this premium model is at its lowest price, and it undercuts some top-end rivals too.

This modest discount on a 4.5-star rated pair of headphones might be enough to sway the needle if you've been considering them. Just note: there's a much better discount on the Stealth 600 available from other retailers, but as far as I can find, that's just on the PS5 model. The Xbox version, like this one, generally isn't reduced by as much.

Logitech's recent premium racing wheel got a near-perfect review from us. The saving isn't massive, but that's because of how recent this model is. $30 off is the first discount for racing gamers who want a top-end piece of kit.

It's impossible to know whether these deals will be beaten over Black Friday, whether it's from Walmart or other retailers. It's very possible that some of these items will go cheaper in the sales, but it's far from guaranteed.

There's another reason to go for these Walmart sales though, and it's all about timing. You see, these discounts are live now, several days ahead of Black Friday, and there's a good chance you'll get them before November 27 (the titular Friday). So you can enjoy them sooner.

Not only that, but items often sell out over Black Friday; buying them now guarantees you'll be able to enjoy the discount. Even if you do get a cheaper item from another retailer in the sales, there's no guarantee you'll receive it in due time. I've heard horror stories of items bought in Black Friday sales taking months to arrive. There's a much lesser chance of that if you buy in advance.

You'll also want to know what the best Xbox Series X accessories are, and keep tabs on the best Black Friday deals for gamers this year, as we'll be constantly updating our round-up.

#3805. Missed something on your first go around The Blood of Dawnwalker? I've got good news, as next week's update adds in new game plus

A big part of the point of The Blood of Dawnwalker is that you're on a fixed time limit. You've got 30 in-game days and nights to try and save your family, and if you don't manage to see everything the game has to offer, well, the game's director is fine with that. But that doesn't matter as much now, as The Blood of Dawnwalker is getting its 1.2 update next week that adds in a new game plus mode.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+!" a post from the devs explains. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over; the level cap will be raised to 100; enemies will be balanced and scale uniformly across all regions; and items will have NG+ versions with updated stats." Sounds like your usual new game plus affair! I suppose it is a good opportunity to try out different things compared to your first playthrough, but I'm not exactly aligned with the idea that the timer restriction is too restricting (as some mods have made clear how others feel that way).

In any case, the update goes a tad further than that. If you got the Eclipse Edition of the game, the in-game soundtrack that came with it "will be extended with additional songs from the game." You can expect the soundtrack on streaming services soon, too. While details are slimmer here, there are also some planned balance changes, like updated enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat, and terrain geometry has seen some improvements to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration."

Overall, a bit of a smaller update compared to the last one, but one I'm sure will be welcome to some all the same. If you've not had a chance to check the game out yet and still feel on the fence about it, here's some lovely words from Mark's review: "There’s always that sense that something important or unexpected could be lurking around the next corner, to pull you into a quest dripping with depth and intrigue. It works to ensure the more busywork-esque tasks attached to angering Brencis and his Boyars never make Vale Sangora feel home to a string of boring boxes to tick. It’s a vibrant, constantly changing place with a thousand different threads metaphorically criss-crossing just beneath its surface, just as ancient ruins literally criss-cross beneath its swamps, crags, and forests."

#3804. "We'd love to have you" - New Zealand's tourist board gives a nod to those hopping timezones to play Grand Theft Auto 6 early

New Zealand's tourism board has taken advantage of all the excitement surrounding Grand Theft Auto 6's launch, as hordes of players who've changed their Xbox timezones to that of the world's second best rugby team (sorry) to jump into the game early.

"One perk of seeing the sun first? Getting GTA 6 first too," reads a post on the New Zealand tourist board's Instagram account: PureNewZealand. "We heard a few of you are trying the New Zealand trick to join us. We get it, and we'd love to have you." The post also includes a video of folks looking at all the natural beauty of New Zealand, presumably before they all look themselves indoors to play the video game, alongside the caption: "life, because we're getting GTA 6 first."

For those unaware, Xbox owners have been swapping their console time zones for years to New Zealand in order to take advantage of the region's access to games before anywhere else in the world. When games have, let's say, a worldwide release time of midnight across all nations, those living in New Zealand are able to jump in first as a result.

Microsoft has for years been happy to let this practice continue on its platform, and as such a sort of cultural norm about hopping on a digital plane for a game's release has been established. If you want guidance, we have a guide on how to pull off the GTA 6 New Zealand trick yourself which can walk you through it.

If you aren't keen on doing so for whatever reason, you can find a breakdown of all the global launch times for GTA 6 too. If you want one final run through on what to expect from Rockstar's big release last minute, our Everything We Know about Grand Theft Auto 6 page should set you right for good measure.

#3803. Poll: Has GTA 6 Lived Up to the Hype Over Its First Weekend?

With GTA 6 launching worldwide last Thursday, I'm hoping that most of you reading this will have spent at least a few hours with the game over the weekend.

As you've no doubt noticed, it's basically been impossible to avoid Rockstar's latest release; here in the online space, it's absolutely everywhere — just as you'd expect of what's supposed to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time.

But has GTA 6 actually lived up to the hype so far? It's no stretch to suggest that this has been the most anticipated video game release ever — but that doesn't mean you have to agree with all of the 10/10 review scores the title was met with last week.

Now, obviously, I'm not asking you to give GTA 6 a review score of your own just yet (although that is coming, don't worry). I'm just wondering if the adventures of Jason and Lucia have met your expectations so far — even if you're only a couple of hours in at this point.

For what it's worth, us here at Push Square have been blown away.

Sammy made his opinion clear in our 10/10 review, of course, but now the rest of us have had a chance to jump in, it's clear that this is an incredibly special game — a generational release.

But it's also clear that GTA 6 is big — really big. For reference, I'm still taking my sweet time on Chapter 1, and the game's scale has already taken me by surprise. I can see myself playing this thing for 100 hours or more quite easily.

(If you don't want to spend upwards of 100 hours playing GTA 6, then our GTA 6 guide may be of use.)

#3802. From 2D to 3D and back to 2D again, the original platforming classic Super Meat Boy returns with a slick remaster complete with new levels and too many old saws

Earlier this year in a bit of a shakeup for the fleshiest kid in town, Super Meat Boy entered into a new dimension in the aptly named Super Meat Boy 3D. I've not played it but it seems like a good take on the format. Clearly, though, sometimes you just need to play the hits, as a new release of the original game is on the way in the form of Super Meat Boy Again+, a remaster with updated graphics, levels and plenty more.

What is there is very clearly Super Meat Boy, uh, again, just with a big new lick of paint. There is probably some kind of joke to be made about it being DLSS yassified, but I'm too tired to think of one, so, you get the point. But it does look pretty good! I do kind of miss the Flash game aesthetic, I think there's a real charm to the sort of visual design sensibilities you'd find from that era, but this remaster certainly ain't ugly at least. Apparently it's not just the art that's new, as there's also new music, cutscenes, secrets and "stuff."

If the animated sequences featured in the trailer, which you can have a gander at above, are included in the final game that'll be a treat to watch too, as I think they better capture the Newgrounds pseudo sub-genre of animation than the graphical overhaul. It sounds like they will be looking at the Steam page, so, a treat to look forward to while committing an act of masochism by playing it!

There's no release date attached to this remaster, so we'll all just have to sit tight for an update there. The original is still listed on Steam, but if you fancy as big a dose of nostalgia as the trailer is trying to present to you, you could always go play the original, plain old regular Meat Boy. It's playable right on Newgrounds thanks to the Flash emulator Ruffle and works like a dream! Or if you're happy to wait, you could always wishlist the new one on Steam.

The sequel to The Witcher 3 is going to change the series

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After three Geralt-centred installments, things are changing a little in The Witcher 4, since Ciri will be the main character instead. This presents a whole other perspective and personal tapestry to the player, and one of the storytelling leads at CD Projekt Red recently spoke on exactly how.

Marcin Blacha, the VP of story at the studio, explained the contrasts between Geralt and Ciri to Inven Global. "Ciri isn't calm and composed like Geralt, nor does she hide her emotions easily," he says. "She is far more hot-headed and tends to be emotional when making decisions. That difference changes a lot of things."

The guiding factor isn't necessarily what's strictly right or wrong, but also how intertwined you've become with any given situation. "When playing as Geralt, players acted more like an arbiter judging how to resolve a situation," Blacha continues. "When playing as Ciri, you are much more deeply involved in the story through her personal perspective."

This impacts the way quests are structured, because CD Projekt Red isn't falling back on the grumpy stoicism of Geralt. "It's no longer just about deciding which choice is morally right; how emotionally invested you are in the character will also shape your decisions," he explains. "Because Ciri is a different person from Geralt, the quests in The Witcher 4 will take on a different shape compared to The Witcher 3."

He notes at the top of his answer that "changing the protagonist is a huge factor," and that goes for all avenues. Geralt is very much the face of the franchise so far, making the jump to Ciri a big creative turn, but she presents all sorts of opportunities for expanding the lore - and the property's reach, too.

After three games, and now yet more DLC for The Witcher 3, Geralt's had plenty of time in the limelight. It's time for someone else to take charge, and it seems like we'll be seeing a whole other side of The Continent in turn.

The Witcher 4 is going to be "an unforgettable experience that's true to the core of the Witcher," narrative lead says as the RPG wins a most-wanted award

#3800. Slay the Spire 2 is one of this year's best selling games despite only being available on PC, and its players are "obsessed"

One million copies for each month on sale, it seems. Slay the Spire 2, Mega Crit's roguelike deckbuilder, is estimated to have sold 7.9m copies since its release in Steam Early Access in March.

That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.

Slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox. That is notable, as the game is only out on Steam, meaning it has sold enough copies to outpace games on platforms it's not even available on.

We already knew Slay the Spire 2 was one of the year's biggest releases. In its first week on sale, the game sold over 3m copies. It quickly became March's top-selling game on Steam, beating blockbuster competition in Crimson Desert and Resident Evil Requiem. Slay the Spire 2, alongside other indie titles such as Meccha Chameleon, have helped Steam deliver another record year of revenue.

It was such a hit, even, that other indie developers felt it negatively impacted sales of their own games. Mewgenics maker Edmund McMillen recently told Eurogamer "it sucked everybody out". "The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over," McMillen said.

Slay the Spire 2 has been consistently popular with players, too, and that popularity has seemingly continued. Elliott noted the game never fell below 2.5 million active players each month since March.

Slay the Spire 2's loyal following also meant that the recently released beta patch, which added a new character, was enough to bring back millions of players. Despite only being available for players who opt into the beta branch of the game, Slay the Spire 2 more than doubled its daily active users to reach its highest daily player count in six months.

"Simply put: Slay the Spire 2 players are obsessed," wrote Elliott. "And it's not just a niche group of dedicated players, either. The average play time is nearly 84 hours, sure. But zooming out, 1.9 million folks have played for over 100 hours."

Incidentally, nearly 100,000 players bought the game but never played it, which Elliott added could explain the discrepancy between player numbers and copies sold.

Looking ahead, Slay the Spire 2's road to version 1.0 is expected to be long, with several features and gameplay additions still in the works. Then there are the console ports, which have yet to be announced, but are very much expected.

In Eurogamer's Slay the Spire 2 early access review, Bertie Purchese called it "a deceptively familiar sequel" whose confident design and smart new additions build on what made the original work so well.

#3799. Congratulations to people who feel mean shooting random NPCs, because GTA 6 tries "to provide mechanisms that encourage" empathy

When you think about GTA as a series, the first thing that probably comes to mind is driving through crowds of people, gunning down whoever you like, just generally doing crime without any care in the world. I wouldn't exactly call it an empathy game, not to say that other games are any better at such a thing anyway. But with GTA 6 out, crikey, next bloody week, a new interview has gone up with co-studio head Rob Nelson where he shared that you have a bit more space to be empathetic compared to previous entries.

"Crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been," Nelson told The Guardian (via @GameRoll_, ta IGN) in a new interview. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out." When asked about whether this will be the first GTA game to encourage people to be empathetic, Nelson responded, "I would say so. I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to."

I am deeply curious as to what those mechanics may be, given that most of what we've seen so far is pretty relegated to shootin', lootin' and a bit of smoochin'. If you steal a car, is there an NPC that loses their job because of it? Can you repair the harm you caused through that action? I'm sure hardly anyone else that's vibrating through their skin in excitement for almost having the game in their fingertips will be asking such questions, I'm just often wary of empathy mechanics in games.

In any case, doesn't matter all that much for us PC lot just yet, especially because Rockstar are preparing themselves both legally and technically to tackle pirated copies of the game. Rockstar will obviously be quite busy at the moment too, not just because of that whole launching a game thing, but because UK-based workers will be voting to unionise as we speak. If formed, it could be 1600 members strong, which would make it the biggest games union in the UK. Solidarity with all the workers as the voting process continues. I hope you get the result you deserve.

#3796. Clair Obscur's narrative lead has left developer Sandfall Interactive after "wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition"

Last night, it was revealed that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's lead narrative designer, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, won a BAFTA Breakthrough US award for her contribution to the hit 2025 game, which made history after winning 12 Game Award nominations last year. In the aftermath of her win, Svedberg-Yen dropped a pretty big bombshell: she's no longer with the game's developer, Sandfall Interactive.

"No, I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition," she told Gamesbeat when asked if she's still with the company. "We've parted ways." As to what Svedberg-Yen is doing next, she offered a cryptic answer, including talk of writing "my own projects, my own stories". She also discussed another project she's set her sights on: establishing a fund to help mentor and grow a new generation of video game narrative designers.

"One of the initiatives I want to build is a narrative investment fund to focus on narrative-focused game creators, trying to bridge the gap between the seed stage and going to publishers," she explained, noting her background working in finance and how that dovetails nicely with her more recent experience as a narrative lead. "This is the chicken and egg question a lot of people face. To get money from publishers you need a demo, but to make a demo you need money. To get money you have to go to publishers. That’s an area where I would like to help a lot of these smaller creatives to get that seed funding so they can, in a way, de-risk themselves in the eyes of bigger investors."

Her motivation for this initiative? Simply, she wants to change how the industry works. "I've discovered that quite a lot of studios don’t really know how to think about narrative, or how to integrate it into their pipelines and their processes. They tend to think it's a very narrow thing, when in fact it can influence all aspects. Part of this would also be an incubation program to help these studios develop those narrative foundations."

"The strongest feeling in me right now for 2027 is I want to help," she added later. "That sounds so cheesy and idealistic. I always cringe at myself for saying it. But I don't know how else to say it and be truthful. I want to help in some way, help the industry."

Sandfall Interactive previously said its guiding "North Star" will always be its "own personal taste", and what the team enjoys.She noted that she didn't think the studio would bow to pressure from fans to do more of the same, but instead be guided by what it thinks is best for itself, and for the series. "I've seen too many TV shows and books be swayed trying to please a lot of people, and in the process you end up losing the heart of what's there," she noted.

We know that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is "not the end" of the franchise, and it seems that whatever happens next, it'll have at least a little bit of Svedberg-Yen's creativity instilled in it. I wish her the best for whatever her next step is.

#3795. Rasen, out in early access now, is a PvP focused take on Dark Souls that borrows one of fighting games' best techy tricks

The idea of Dark Souls PvP has always scared me a tad. You can replace Dark Souls with Bloodborne or Elden Ring, I've typically just been a coward when it comes to the idea of fighting another, real person. They're probably going to be better than me! I don't use tactics in Souls games, I use brute force until I get my way! That being said, I do have to admit I quite like the look of Rasen, a game that is essentially just the PvP component of Dark Souls (or PvE if you just want to take on some computer-controlled enemies) that just launched into early access.

To say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things. For one, it looks more like it leans a tad towards Sekiro with a blades-only kind of affair, whether that be big or small. And blades a plenty they have, ranging from your classic sword, to scythes, to halberds and all sorts. It's a much flashier looking affair too, with fancy slashing effects that seem to buff moves and a pace that seems much faster than Souls games tend to be.

You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat! And best of all, unusually for a 3D arena fighter, it has rollback netcode. For those unfamiliar, and to try and explain it simply, this is essentially a bit of tech you'll find in predominantly 2D fighting games that predicts every possible input you could make in a given moment, helping to reduce lag time and allow for tighter matches (and less rage quitting).

That's a bit harder to do in a 3D environment given that you have a lot more options at your disposal when it comes to movement, so if it works that's some impressive stuff! And we could all quite easily find out together, as a demo for Rasen is available to try out. Or, alternatively, you can just pick it up whole hog on Steam right now, as it's available in early access.

#3794. Guide: GTA 6: Tenebrae Lux Walkthrough & Puzzle Solutions

Early on in GTA 6, you'll gain access to the JoySystem, a game console with a handful of games you can play. One of those is Tenebrae Lux, a black and white, first-person puzzle game. In this GTA 6 guide, we have a Tenebrae Lux walkthrough, guiding you through the puzzles to reach the ending.

Tenebrae Lux features randomised elements in some of its puzzles, so your experience may vary from what you see in our images and videos.

On this page: GTA 6: Tenebrae Lux Walkthrough & Puzzle Solutions

Below is our walkthrough of Tenebrae Lux, revealing puzzle solutions and where to find notes.

There are 11 notes to collect in total, but the last two require you to collect the previous nine.

In a single playthrough of Tenebrae Lux, you can find those 9 notes hidden in 17 possible locations. Collecting these 9 notes will then allow you to find the 10th and 11th notes.

After waking up on the island, you must solve at least three grid-based puzzles located on the beach, though there are five to find in total — two of which are necessary if you're looking for every note.

Awaken on the beach and make your way to the shelter on the horizon, as pictured:

Go inside the shelter and head for the wooden boxes directly opposite the entrance:

On the table you'll find Note Location #1, as pictured:

Immediately next to Note Location #1 is a board you can interact with. This is Board Puzzle #1.

As is the case with all the other Board Puzzles, Board Puzzle #1 is randomly selected from a batch of puzzles; you won't always be presented with the same one.

To solve the puzzle, follow the steps in the below videos depending on which puzzle you have in front of you:

In the same area as Board Puzzle #1, you'll find Board Puzzle #2 just to the right of the entrance as you enter. For context, the location is pictured:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After solving the first two Board Puzzles, you should make your way to the next shack along. First, though, check between them to find an upturned boat on the beach:

This is Note Location #2, where you'll find the note leaning against the boat:

After checking Note Location #2, go inside the shack:

On the right-hand side are some hooks; this is Note Location #3, where you may find a note hanging with some rope and a set of scales:

After checking Note Location #2, enter the shelter to the right. This is what it looks like:

Go inside through the front entrance, as shown:

Head towards the wooden crate at the back-right part of the building:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After solving Board Puzzle #3, turn around and leave the shack through the door ahead:

Turn right and inspect the railing; this is Note Location #4, where you may find a note on the railing:

After checking Note Location #4, go around to the front of the shack, where you entered the first time:

To the right of the entrance are a couple of crates; this is Note Location #5, where you may find a note resting against the crates:

After solving Board Puzzle #3, exit the shelter and go left along the coast (it's quite a walk):

You will pass a small dock with a door on it to your left, ignore it and continue forward:

Here you'll find Board Puzzle #4 next to a shipping container:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After solving Board Puzzle #4, the shipping container directly next to it will unlock:

Inside is Note Location #6 , with the note leaning against the back:

After collecting the note at Note Location #4, walk all the way back where you came from, then go up to the shack on the raised area:

Go around to the back of the shack to find Board Puzzle #5:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After completing Board Puzzle #5, turn to your left and go inside the shack:

On the right-hand side is a small table, where you'll find Note Location #7:

After checking Note Location #7, exit the shack and look across the island to find a door in the distance with three lights above it:

Inside is Note Location #8, where there are several crates in which the note may appear:

After checking Note Location #6, go through the door ahead and up the stairs:

You'll come to a room with several things you must pay attention to in order to solve this next puzzle. You'll need to make some notes!

The goal is to input the correct string of numbers into the telephone on the back wall. However, there is no defined phone number for you to use; it is a randomised solution.

To learn the phone number, you must pass through several incarnations of the same room to discover differences in the environment, one by one.

Upon first entering the room, you'll see the text "DEVELOPED USING ZUCHWORKS ENGINE" followed by a Greek letter:

It could be any of the following letters, and each corresponds to a numerical value which you must make a note of:

From the left-hand side and moving clockwise around the room, you may find the following things to inspect:

Vinyl records: Make a note of the price and the RPM values. Add the digits together, e.g. if the price is 50 cents, 5+0=0. Same goes for the RPM:

Lamp: When you enter the room, it will flash a morse code message. Decipher it using the chart located on the right of the console

Wall clock: Make a note of the time, and work out the clockwise angle from the hour to the minute hand. Add the digits of the angle together for the appropriate number (e.g. 2 o'clock, angle 300°, 3+0+0=3):

Calendar: The dates 6th and 31st are circled. More on the calendar later:

Phone ringing: When you enter the room, the phone will ring a certain number of times — note down how many

Framed picture: Make a note of how many figures you can see in the picture:

Emergency Protocols: Make a note of the number of the document. It may be redacted:

Cassette tape: Make a note of the date stated when you play the tape recorder:

Wall picture: The picture shows Roman numerals depicted by pillars — note the number

Once you've noted all of the above, proceed through the door next to the phone and up the stairs. You will find yourself in a new iteration of the same room.

The idea now is to inspect everything again, including the onscreen text with the Roman letter, to search for an anomaly. When you find a number that is different from your notes from the original room, note it down.

For example: In the original room, the framed picture showed 3 people, but in the next room, the picture shows 4 people. Note down '4'.

Observe the calendar; it will now have many dates scratched out:

The first date that's clear after the 6th October correlates with the anomaly you have discovered.

So, make a note of your anomaly and the date, then go through the door again, and repeat until you have found anomalies against the following dates:

If done correctly, you should now have a six-digit number to punch into the phone. In the order of the dates, enter the number followed by '#' to solve the puzzle:

While you're working on the Bunker Puzzle, check the crate on the left-hand side of the room:

This is Note Location #9, where you may find a note inside the crate:

After checking Note Location #9, look on the other side of the room to see a valve on the wall:

This is Note Location #10, where you may find a note just behind the valve:

After completing the Bunker's puzzle, go through the door by the phone one last time and you'll emerge in a new room:

This is Note Location #11, where you may find a note on top of one of the flat carts:

After checking Note Location #11, head outside to the right:

After the first set, look left to find this note, as pictured:

After checking Note Location #12, continue towards some ruins:

On the right, there is a post with a light next to it — this is Note Location #13, where you may find a note atop the post:

After checking Note Location #13, go around to the right-hand side of the ruins:

On the right-hand side is an open crate; this is Note Location #14, where you may find a note inside the crate:

After checking Note Location #14, walk through the ruins to the back, where you can see a pulley system:

There is a closed crate next to it; this is Note Location #15, where a note may appear on the crate:

After checking Note Location #15, return to the front of the ruins and you'll see a plaque with a poem on it (yours may be different to the one pictured):

The poem contains particular words in each line that correspond to the objects you will find in the ruins. The exact locations of these objects are randomised.

Your goal in this puzzle is to cross the bridge towards the lighthouse, walking across glowing symbols in the correct order:

As mentioned, aspects of this puzzle are random, so there is no definite solution.

To discover the correct path across the bridge, you must locate each of the following items, then cross-reference them with your poem to decipher the right order of the symbols.

Brazier (Related poem words: Furnace, Scorch, Heat, Fire, Flames, Fiery):

Fountain (Related poem words: Water, Drink, River, Lakes, Wetlands, Swamps):

Moon Sculpture (Related poem words: Moon, Moonshine, Lunar, Evening, Night, Sleep):

Sundial (Related poem words: Sun, Sunlight, Solar, Sunrise):

Tree (Related poem words: Forest, Woods, Rest):

Trophy (Related poem words: Gold, Riches, Trove, Treasure, Prize):

Vase (Related poem words: Earth, Soil, Ground, Mound):

When you find one of these objects, you must then enter the ruins and observe the object through an opposite archway; the symbol at the top of the arch corresponds to that object. For example:

To recap, you need to do three things to get the answer to cross the bridge:

Once you have this all lined up, approach the bridge and cross the correct symbols in the correct order:

After successfully crossing the bridge (or before you cross it), go back across it towards the ruins, where you just came from:

Find the Brazier in the ruins and walk into it. The character will talk about the tattoo on his hand if you've done it right:

Now go across the bridge again and approach the small hut to the right. It will only unlock if you do the above steps first:

Go inside and you'll find this note on a chair:

After getting the note from Note Location #16, follow the path up to the lighthouse:

Go up the steps on the left side of the lighthouse:

At the top, look right to find this note on the postbox:

As soon as you have collected a total of 9 notes, make your way back to the bunker's phone room. To the left of the console is another door that's now unlocked:

Go inside, and go to the person on the bed:

Beneath him you can observe another note, depicting various phases of the moon:

These moon symbols also appear on the calendar in the phone room, so go back out and check it:

You need to find the dates that match the symbols on the note to create a string of numbers. If the dates have two digits, add them together to make one.

The sequence of symbols and where they appear on the calendar are randomised, so your solution will be different for each playthrough.

In this example, the solution is 2, 2, 1, 1, 6, 3, followed by #.

When you have your number sequence, go to the phone and enter it:

If you've done it correctly, the man on the bed will be gone and you can pick up the note:

After solving the moon symbols puzzle and collecting your 10th note, stay in the bunker's phone room as you have one more number to dial:

Open Tenebrae Lux's pause menu with Touch Pad and select Notes:

Here, you can look at all 10 of your collected notes. Each of them represents a number, as follows:

Your goal is to create another string of numbers based on the order in which your notes appear in your Notes menu. This is random.

So, using the above images as reference and following their order on the Notes menu, create your number sequence, then dial it into the phone, followed by '#':

If you've done it correctly, a cryptic message will play regarding the final note.

The last, 11th note can now be found on the bridge to the lighthouse — walk back there and search the bridge for the note:

It might appear on the railings or on the pillars at either end of the bridge.

Now that you have collected all 11 notes in Tenebrae Lux, there is one more puzzle waiting for you. Open the Notes menu again and you'll find that the first 10 notes now each have a word in bold somewhere on them:

These words are each associated with a number, based on the Kabbalah Tree of Life (unrelated to the game). Here's how it breaks down:

Using this information, you need to put together another number sequence. For example, if the second note in your Notes menu represents #9, and has the word Victory on it (representing 7), the seventh number in your sequence will be 9.

Once you have your number sequence, you need to dial it into the bunker's phone, so go back there if you're not there already:

If you enter the numbers correctly, you will hear another message. Exit the bunker back down onto the beach, and walk back towards the shipping container:

On the way is a small dock with a door on it — you can now enter the door:

Approach the desk and interact with the computer to begin a speedrunning challenge, in which you must complete Tenebrae Lux within 20 minutes.

You don't have to do all this business with the notes again — just get to the lighthouse and complete its puzzle to finish.

After collecting Note #4, go back down the stairs and in through the door at the base of the lighthouse:

You will be presented with a series of doors:

You gotta hand it to them, but the payout sounds like it would have been small potatoes to the company.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

James Lowder, a freelance writer and editor who has contracted with Wizards of the Coast on D&D books, discussed the news and its personal impact on him via LinkedIn. Here's the second half of Lowder's post, explaining the mechanics of how this came about:

"This is remarkable and amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars that WotC could have collected going to the writers. And Wizards is doing this at a time when the larger publishers are scrambling to grab as much settlement money as possible from authors. Amazing. This payout will help a lot of writers--folks who certainly deserve to be rewarded for their work.

"Conversations at Wizards about the Anthropic settlement have been ongoing for months. (I've been part of these conversations on and off, but the real heavy lifting was done by folks with more clout.) This all came about because some of the writers used what influence they possessed to raise the issue and because the people inside Wizards, up to the highest levels, were willing to consider the situation from more than a financial perspective.

"Thanks to all the writers who stepped up here. I don't think this would have happened without those author-prompted discussions, especially the efforts of R.A. Salvatore. Huge credit to the folks at Wizards, in particular Dan Ayoub, who were open to the discussions and then did the generous (and right) thing here. And it was the right thing to do."

It is unambiguously great that writers like Lowder benefitted from this settlement more than they were required to⁠—it's the spiritual opposite of all the companies that pocketed their tariff refunds instead of passing them onto the consumers who ate inflated prices. The authors who make D&D great deserve it. You do gotta hand it to Wizards.

But. In the interest of providing full context, I have to be a cynical prick for the remainder of this article. Wizards of the Coast's reputation has taken a drubbing in recent years, and even though D&D and Magic are practically synonymous with tabletop and TCGs respectively, it behooves the company to secure PR victories like this where it can.

Most recently, Wizards has refused to voluntarily recognize an employee union twice in one year, forcing a vote among the staff. The results of the ballot are not yet public, but Wargamer reported last week that the company appears to be preparing to deal with a unionised workforce.

Moving back in time, Wizards' attempt to rework D&D's influential Open Gaming License (OGL) met a huge fan and industry backlash, prompting the company to backpedal almost immediately. Contemporaneously, incidents of AI art appearing in marketing material and a D&D sourcebook similarly met with a sour response.

And the whopper: Wizards of the Coast laid off 1,100 people in 2023, including much of the publishing team that liaised with Larian Studios on Baldur's Gate 3. Larian has insisted that its decision to pivot from D&D back to its own Divinity series was a creative one, and that its shift away from Wizards was amicable, but most forum-goers and hoi polloi still assume the worst about the split.

Lowder's estimate that Wizards stood to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars here also stood out to me⁠—that's life-changing money for you, me, or even an extremely successful author like R.A. Salvatore, but it's couch cushion change for a multi-billion dollar operation like Wizards of the Coast. The real value of the case to publishers, by my reckoning, was extracting some sort of concession, a legal precedent regarding copyright and training AI models. Wizards of the Coast undeniably did the right thing here, but I think it was a PR victory cheaply bought.

#3792. Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - founded by ex-GTA veteran - has a mountain of debt, and the main plan for paying it back is litigation

"A coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary."

Beleaguered Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - the company created by former Rockstar and Grand Theft Auto producer Leslie Benzies - apparently owes approximately £62 million in debt. And a huge chunk of that appears to be owed to Chinese gaming company NetEase (£36.5m), though more than £1m appears to be owed to Benzies himself.

This came to light in a proposal issued by Build a Rocket Boy's administrators this week (spotted by Resetera), which lists both the moneys owed (right down to a £20 charge to OpenAI) and details what went wrong, as well as what Build a Rocket Boy intends to do to recoup money to pay the debts back. And the company's "largest" potential asset, according to the administrators, is litigation.

"Prior to the Company's entry into Administration, the directors had been investigating circumstances surrounding the commercial performance of the video game, MindsEye, which was released in 2025 following significant development investment," the administration proposal read. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary.

"The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that any such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions."

This tallies with the narrative spun by co-company leader Mark Gerhard as the company waded into deep water. Gerhard blamed "organised espionage and corporate sabotage" for the studio's difficulties as multiple rounds of layoffs shredded Build a Rocket Boy. "People had their hands on the scale and deliberately tried to shape a negative narrative around the product," Gerhard said.

The situation he's referring to is likely the alleged smear campaign made against the game, which Gerhand reportedly claimed in an internal meeting this year was paid for by a "big American company" and then run by a UK company called Ritual Network, which apparently had influencers, journalists and staff at Build a Rocket Boy deliberately sabotage the game's release. That's according to an account of a videoed internal meeting reportedly seen by Insider Gaming earlier this year.

It had nothing to do with the dire state of Mindseye when it launched, then. Eurogamer awarded it one out of five stars, chastising its "ridiculous story, inconsistent writing, poorly designed mission scenarios, and utterly atrocious combat" in our Mindseye review.

Build a Rocket Boy was founded in 2016, and its first game, Everywhere - a sort of online gaming platform - was announced in 2022. It never materialised, but a part of that vision was carved out to become a standalone game experience of its own along the way, and that's how we got Mindseye - a take on a Grand Theft Auto formula. Whether or not the litigation is successful and can recoup any of Build a Rocket Boy's debts remains to be seen, but there's a financial mountain for the studio to climb if it hopes to operate again.

When most reviews and the majority of fan feedback for a game is positive, I think it's safe to say you're in for a treat – and that's the case with this Lord of the Rings card game series. Its reputation in the hobby is glowing, enough to make the Arkenstone seem dim by comparison.

It can be hard to put a fresh and exciting spin on something that's been around for 72 years, but this trick-taking Lord of the Rings card game manages it. Using classic, time-tested mechanics but providing a very clever cooperative spin on them, it's a fresh approach to the story. Love Middle-earth? You owe it to yourself to try this, because the series is worthy of standing amongst the best card games. As an example, 87% of user reviews for the first one (Fellowship of the Ring Trick-Taking Game) are a full five stars at Amazon.

The first game in this series establishes the rules, so I'd definitely begin here. It's currently sitting at a record-low price over at Amazon, and has never been cheaper than it is now. Because it also has a Black Friday deals badge, I doubt it'll be available for less either.

Once you've finished the first entry in the series, you can graduate to the second one (which we gave five stars in our Two Towers Trick-Taking Game review). While you can technically begin here, it builds on the mechanics of the first entry, so it isn't the best starting point.

As a trick-taking game, the lead player puts down a numbered card, and everyone else has to match that suit (Hills, Mountains, Forests, Shadows, or Rings) with the highest number possible. Whoever has the highest score wins the round, but it's not just about clearing your hand of cards. Every character has a unique objective they've got to complete, from winning the fewest rounds to earning Ring cards. Because you only complete a chapter if everyone's objective is complete, there's an extra tactical layer to navigate.

That's especially true because players are only allowed to discuss cards that have been put down during setup or play. You can't explain what you have in your hand or anything beyond your character's goal either, so you've got to hope everyone else understands what you're trying to do based on the cards you're playing. It's a novel challenge, and it only gets more interesting with each chapter of the game. You see, it regularly adds extra complications to keep you on your toes.

While the series isn't finished yet, it will be soon – the third and final entry, Return of the King, is due to launch on January 15, 2027. It promises "new gameplay twists that create fresh strategic decisions for both new and returning players," and considering how novel the previous two are, that should be worth getting excited about.
