#3729. The hunt for World of Warcraft: Forever secrets continue with the discovery of an elusive pet

The search for secrets in World of Warcraft: Forever continues ever onwards, with a new breakthrough coming to light in recent days. The latest discovery? An elusive new cat that can be tamed by hunters in one of the game's new zones.

The cat's name is Ta'Shkal, and they can be found on Mount Hyjal. An endgame levelling zone, players will have to reach at least level 57 in order to safely make their way up there and recruit this new pet.

The way you do so is relatively simple. You need to find a small corrupted cat figuring within the Felblood Scar region of Mount Hyjal. Once you've found that, you then need to travel up to a hidden lantern south of the Mourning's Rest area. With the figurine in your bags, you'll be able to interact with the lantern, spawning the cat for you to tame (granted you're playing a hunter).

So what's the big deal about this cat? Well, aside from the fact it's got a strange colour scheme of green fur with orange stripes, the cat also has a base attack speed of 1.0. This means it'll attack once every second, which is pretty fast and allows for greater damage output from your pet. This inherently makes the pet valuable for endgame hunter players, who are looking to improve their performance in PvE and PvP.

This is not the only secret discovered by World of Warcraft: Forever sleuths. Last week, they pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. As of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

The game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among new and returning players. It's the biggest launch in the series' history, and has gone down well with people so far. Even if it has recently suffered its first controversy with a now-fixed gold exploit.

I'd just stolen my very first airplane in GTA 6 and was happily cruising over the city when I looked out my window and saw an enormous purple building. I banked, slowed down, and flew a bit closer to read the huge sign on the roof.

Oh, hell yes. I was so excited to throw my carefully accumulated three hundred dollars away on poker and slots that I immediately attempted my very first landing. After the explosion and my miraculous resurrection, I rushed back to the casino and crashed again, this time with my body into the locked front doors.

The casino in GTA 6 is closed. Trust me, I tried every door, and the only one that opened was a utility closet.

I was early into my playthrough, still in Chapter 1 of the GTA 6 story missions, so I thought maybe there'll be some mission that unlocks the casino so I can play some poker, try my luck at the slots, and maybe bet on the also-closed dog track—I assume it's a dog track because I've seen dogs in GTA 6, but no horses—that's right next door to the casino.

Nope! I'm now 100% done with the main story and that casino is still closed. And that's not the only business in GTA 6 that isn't open for business. Not even a half-mile away from the casino there's a go-cart track called Hot Skidz sporting a huge "Coming Soon" sign. I saw that early in my game as well, and checked back later. Still closed. I also found a second, smaller casino. Also closed.

What a letdown. I managed to get my motorcycle onto the go-cart track, and as I drove glumly around it, alone, having no fun, I perked up a bit. Maybe this just gives me something to look forward to. A hint of more singleplayer content that'll be coming to GTA 6 next year. Hopefully next year.

There's already a lot of seemingly unfinished stuff in GTA 6, partial systems that could be added to and completed, like:

I felt better after that, but as I went back to stare at that huge, closed casino—which is all lit up at night like it's actually open, even though it is not open, and I know this because I rechecked all the doors—I remembered how the casino in GTA 5 worked. It came to the game post launch, but only as part of GTA Online. It never opened in singleplayer.

But surely, why include the building at all in GTA 6 singleplayer if it wasn't also going to be in singleplayer? They wouldn't do that to us, would they? They wouldn't open it in GTA 6 Online and not open it in GTA 6 singleplayer.

That would be like putting dozens of dogs in a game and not letting us have our own dog. Madness.

#3725. GameStop CEO slams 'code-in-a-box' games in the wake of GTA 6's discless release

"The decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers."

Ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs. Per the CEO, the industry's move away from physical games and towards a digital-only future is harmful to both consumers and businesses.

In an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend. Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop."

These comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch. The game, expected to be the biggest video game launch of all time, is not shipping on discs at all. Even if you purchase a physical copy of the game, what you will actually take home is a 'code in a box' - giving you a code you can redeem on your console of choice that entitles you to a digital version of the game. GTA 6 is not the first game to do this, but it is the most high-profile. Similarly to discs, codes are also region-locked (at least on the PS5), meaning that the proliferation of codes as a format isn't even helping make games more readily available in certain markets.

Cohen notes he's been in conversation with "the obvious [publishers]" but that he's had little sway on their plans. "Of course they don’t like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying new," he told Bloomberg. "They're taking away competition."

Though Cohen doesn't name GTA 6 specifically in the Bloomberg interview, it's clear that he's talking about Rockstar's megaton launch (he explicitly tweeted "GTA. On a disc. In a case. On your shelf. Like if you still want a physical copy" two days ago). The lack of trade-in potential is clearly harming his business; the Bloomberg article reveals pre-owned and refurbished products make up 22% of the GameStop's sales, down 32 percent from the same time a year ago.

Of course, the proliferation of game-in-a-box products doesn't end with GTA 6. Sony plans to stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation games starting in January 2028, moving to a digital-only model despite pushback from consumers and certain developers and publishers. The outcry is doing little to influence Sony's decision, however.

Disc or no disc, GTA 6 is expected to cross $2bn in its opening weekend, and at the moment that is looking like a conservative figure, too. It's estimated the game has sold well over 19.05m units at the time of writing. Despite the astronomical sales, though, employees at Rockstar are still worried about layoffs. Additionally, a tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members (who were fired for apparent breaches of their NDAs) just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3724. "Games are best made by people": The IWGB and other European unions publish joint manifesto calling on workers, employers and consumers to reject genAI

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people."

The manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture."

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games."

It's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable."

Grand Theft Auto 6 has been out in the hands of console players for a few days now, and a few of us at PC Gamer have been dusting off our PlayStations and Xboxes to dive into Leonida as we eagerly anticipate its eventual (but yet unannounced) PC release next year potentially.

I've been gaming it up myself and, as is always the case with GTA, I am absolutely loving driving around. Flying down the highway, exploring all the alleyways and retail areas, and taking out to the waters on a boat or jetski. All of it, of course, to the soundtrack of GTA 6's various radio stations.

There are a huge number of stations in this game—19 of them, to be exact—with a ton of excellently-curated songs lingering within and famous cameo hosts. Usually I find myself just picking one station and sticking to it, but with GTA 6? I've been cycling between quite a few, each one offering something a little bit different.

Four stations have been grabbing most of my attention though. Pop station Flash FM has easily gained the most airtime in my playthrough so far. Am I listening to Ariana Grande in my everyday life? No. But am I bombing it down the highway while singing Break Free to myself every time it comes on? I absolutely am.

But I've also been peppering in a ton of 80s station Vice City FM. I mean, c'mon, you've got Weird Al Yankovic as a co-host, first of all. But you've also got straight up bangers like Lionel Richie's All Night Long, Simply Red's Money's Too Tight (To Mention), and Billy Ocean's Loverboy.

There's also Emotion 98.3, the radio station dedicated to songs about love (both being in love and being heartbroken, of course) and yes, I have stayed in the car waiting to hear Phil Collins' excellent drumming in In The Air Tonight. And finally, because I am a raging emo at heart, I've obviously had to whack on a bunch of The Chamber 106.6. Tool, System of a Down, and Metallica? Count me in.

But what about you? If any of you PC gamers are partaking on console, is only one radio station catching your attention, or have you found yourself channel hopping just like me? Or is there somehow not a single station that's caught your fancy, instead finding the podcasts a more entertaining use of your listening time? Be sure to drop a comment and let me know.

Huang says "I am grateful for the love and support of my family"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia CEO, president, and board director by the company's board. The vote on Huang's return, which comes just weeks after his resignation amid a scandal over allegedly multiple affairs, was unanimous following unspecified but telling "input from senior levels of the United States government."

In a press release published today, Nvidia's board is suddenly flush with praise of Huang, the unfaithful man they only just fired out of a cannon. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia says. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."

Huang himself, who recently said he would be more than happy to return to one of the highest-paying jobs imaginable, also commented on his reinstatement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," he insists.

Before anything, Huang says, "I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period."

Huang adds, "I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work.”

A recent New York Times report details extensive allegations of abusive conduct against Huang, with multiple sources saying he regularly threatened employees with violence and used public humiliation to impose his will. His actions reportedly included threatening to tear one employee's arms off, threatening to crack another's skull open and urinate on their brain, mocking an employee for spending time with their family, and telling an elderly employee that people are hoping for their death.

With Nvidia stock plunging in recent weeks and the company at the center of much of the AI data center buildout propping up both the US economy's growth and the stock market's outsized tech sector, US President Donald Trump has repeatedly called for the return of Huang in television and social media statements. "I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back," Trump said just days ago.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Trump reacted to Huang's reinstatement in real-time on Truth social, dismissing claims of Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct," he says. This administration is, of course, famous for treating unfaithful leaders with kid gloves.

Nvidia also addresses this more directly. "As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation," the board writes. "The Board reiterated that the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it."

A newly formed counsel within Nvidia will also now oversee "trade compliance and national security risks."

On the heels of this news, Nvidia's stock has jumped from a November 20 close of 125.53 to, at the time of writing, 166.82 and climbing, per Yahoo.

Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney says Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepping down amid multiple affair allegations marks "a sad day for Nvidia, developers, America, and all humanity."

#3720. I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that big a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in New York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

Sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

You could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

They often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

The latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

They aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

#3719. GTA 6 has replaced websites with social media and phone apps because "it didn't feel necessary"

The internet of today is a far cry from the days when Grand Theft Auto 5 was released, which is partly why Rockstar didn't bring back its own satirical version of the web in GTA 6.

The web pages of Lifeinvadder, Bleeter, and Eyefind have instead given way to BuckMe, Scooter Bros, and WhatUp apps. The reason? Smartphone apps just made more sense.

"It didn't feel necessary for us," Rockstar North boss Rob Nelson told Kotaku. "We definitely wanted to lean into apps and create these apps."

Though some of the apps in GTA 6 perform similar tasks to the web of old, Nelson said the team didn't want players to be distracted from the game's detailed open world by staring at screens. That also extends to getting players to appreciate the value of money, and witnessing the progression of Jason and Lucia as they go from pawnshop robberies to staging major bank heists.

"They don't really need websites to be buying a lot of shit, you know what I mean, and so everything grows very organically," Nelson said, adding that websites may return in the future.

"I remember asking Stu Petri, our head of 2D and UI, about websites, and he was like, 'For what? What do you need it for?' So, that was it," he added.

In materials supplied by Rockstar ahead of our review, Sam Grosset (associate UI director at the studio) also explained that a lot of thought went into how the apps work, and how easily the phone needed to fit into your play style in order for it to work as effectively as possible.

"We ensure the UI feels like a natural extension of the game world, supporting players without interrupting gameplay or breaking immersion, unless necessary to do so," said Grosset. "The UI should be complementary to the game and appropriate for each scenario. It was a big shift for our phone interface to be in-hand, but it supports that feeling of playing as Jason or Lucia and helps us stay embedded in the world."

Rockstar would continually "raise the bar, question assumptions, explore new possibilities, and learn through rigorous testing and iteration" in order to make these apps - and the UX/UI in general - feel in line with the production quality of the rest of the game.

In Eurogamer's GTA 6 review, Chris Tapsell awarded the open-world crime game five stars, raving about its absurd level of detail, compelling characters, exciting action and of its big heart.

If you're looking to spend the next several days playing Rockstar's latest hit, Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough has detailed guides on everything from individual missions, to core mechanics like the new Wanted Level, and relationship and romance.

If you ever watch science videos on social media, you've probably been served a video of someone debunking the claims of a flat earther.

It starts with a clip of some belligerent dope demanding to know why, if the earth is so round, ships don't disappear over the horizon. A greenscreened science communicator then appears, rubs their forehead, and shows us a video of a ship disappearing over the horizon. Checkmate.

It's good content, but if you linger too long on one of those videos, you'll get another, and then another, and pretty soon your whole feed will be debunking videos. Now you're enrolled in a never ending lesson plan which features such insights as 'an all-meat diet is not good for you,' 'the moon landing was real,' and 'hating women is not in fact based.'

The total effect of this is that the most ignorant and dishonest quacks and provocateurs get to set the level of discourse, and instead of investigating new metaphorical horizons in topics that interest you, you wind up watching people debate the existence of the actual horizon.

Which brings me to Grand Theft Auto 6. Despite making $3.79 billion on its launch day, it's easy to stumble across confident social media claims that it's a total flop and everyone's going to refund it. According to popular X posts, GTA 6 doesn't even let you steal cars anymore, and there are hundreds of Metacritic user reviewers insisting that it's far-left propaganda rather than the mass-market entertainment product it obviously is.

It's the videogame discourse version of flat eartherism. The millions of people playing GTA 6 do not think it is a "cuck simulator" because you can buy a woman flowers, but it's hard not to react to the few dorks making that claim, even though focusing on debunking them severely limits the depth of the conversations we can then have about the game. Good luck discussing your feelings if you dislike GTA 6 for normal reasons!

Over the past few days, I've entertained sparks of hope that GTA 6 could be the flashpoint that brings us out of this era of videogame discourse. The millions of people playing it and not reacting like buffoons are surely irrefutable evidence that culture war dunces don't represent the masses.

But then again, we're still pointing at videos of ships going over the horizon to prove that the earth isn't flat.

#3716. Former Dishonored designer joins the team on New Blood's Victorian immersive sim Gloomwood, with a new level and new weapons coming this year

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by New Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The update is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

GTA 6's first post-launch update is here, with Rockstar Games rolling out fixes for a number of annoying issues and, perhaps most importantly, seemingly leaving a couple of cool glitches alone.

Patch 01.002.002 or 1.0.2.2, depending on which platform you're on, is out now across PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and per the patch notes, there are a number of key improvements.

First of all, several crash fixes should stop you from being booted out of Leonida unprompted, and "an issue that resulted in the game not autosaving correctly" should make doubly sure that you won't randomly lose too much progress in the game going forward.

Certain in-game phone calls weren't triggering correctly throughout missions and the story, and those should now be fixed. "An issue that resulted in the players being unable to lose their Wanted Level" has been ironed out too, so you can get back to your crime sprees (or fun-loving life in Leonida) without having to constantly watch your back for the cops.

Notably, there's no mention in the patch notes of the fun glitch that can force the game into an unintended first-person perspective, nor the Xbox glitch that can make GTA 6 run at 60fps, so it looks like players will still be able to have fun with those for now.

Interestingly, it sounds like we can expect to see more varied weather in the game going forward, too. I've seen a lot of chatter about how it never seems to rain in Leonida, and in today's patch notes, Rockstar says: "Fixed an issue that resulted in the weather not changing for extended periods." So, it sounds like the near-constant sunshine might not have been intentional after all.

It'd be wrong to describe Rockstar's latest as bug-ridden by any means – there's a reason why so many GTA 6 reviews have awarded it a perfect score – but there's inevitably always room for improvement and further fine-tuning. I just hope we might get an overhaul to the wonky money withdrawal and deposit system for Jason's stash and the ATMs – please, Rockstar, just let us type in the amount we want to move.

#3714. Embracer begin yet another round of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, while they're still midway through development on two Tomb Raider games

Update: Studio confirms eight staff lost their jobs

Update 18/11: Crystal Dynamics have provided the following statement to RPS, confirming it cut eight staff members:

As initially reported by Vertical Slice (thanks, Chris!), the workforce of Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics is being cut as part of a new set of layoffs by owners Embracer. As far as is currently known, those affected include senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, and UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, all of whom shared news of their redunancies on LinkedIn. There may be more affected, but neither Crystal Dynamics nor Embracer have offered comments on the reduction of staff as yet.

This now marks the studio's fifth round of layoffs since Embracer acquired it in 2022, following cuts in March 2025, August 2025, November 2025, and March this year. This is a drastic amount even considering the current state of the industry, with layoffs seemingly happening several times a week, but unfortunately, this is par for the course for Embracer. Even still, it makes one wonder just how many staff are left at Crystal Dynamics by now. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis and Tomb Raider: Catalyst are still in production, so you'd hope that the studio won't be shuttered entirely.

According to Legacy of Atlantis' Steam page, generative AI has been used in the development of Legacy of Atlantis "to support some early exploration and temporary development content. Any AI-assisted assets were either replaced or refined by humans in order to maintain the creative and artistic vision of the development team." I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

The longest game of Dota I've played was comfortably past the 70-minute mark. Matches that gloriously long-winded can be fun in small doses, but they can also be exhausting and infuriating—this is Dota we're talking about, after all. The latest patch to rearrange the venerable MOBA, 7.42, is finally here, and it's got tons of changes that might just prevent your games from going feature length.

The most exciting of these, for my money, is the Greater Horn of Battle: a guaranteed drop from the Tormentor neutral monster that summons a wave of super creeps in all your team's lanes (the patch notes refer to them as the more powerful mega creeps, but players have noted the stats don't match up that way). If you've played League of Legends or Deadlock, it fills a niche similar to the Rift Herald or Deadlock's Unstable Rifts—an objective you can complete in the earlier stages of a game to push lane(s) hard.

It's an ability that, if timed correctly, could force the other team to scramble to protect each lane or risk losing lots of ground. And it's not the only change with the potential to speed up matches.

Base hero health has gone up from 120 to 200, with the caveat that strength now gives less health per point, meaning that heroes will be sturdier early on but slightly squishier later. The Glyph of Fortification, a teamwide spell that makes buildings invulnerable, no longer resets its cooldown when certain buildings go down. Heroes also now gain experience passively, even when dead, meaning that you never completely stop growing stronger as the match progresses.

It will probably take some time to see if this actually meaningfully reduces match times or if these changes even stick around for long, but personally, anything that makes Dota a little bit speedier has the potential to reignite my passion for the game. Whenever I dip in these days, it's to play the fastest mode possible—Turbo, which accelerates every aspect of play and gives you oodles of gold just for existing—but it's so different from the traditional Dota setup that it may as well be a new game.

#3711. Sony defeat $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit which argued PlayStation's dominant market position fuels "excessive and unfair" game prices

It's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the company of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

It's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

In a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

As if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another big game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

The final Avengers: Doomsday trailer has arrived, and it's massive

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's almost time. The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday is finally here, and it's packed full of exciting, chills-inducing moments.

In all the fun, though, you might have missed a few details that jumped out at us. That's where we come in. Below, we've broken down the 14 biggest details in the new Avengers: Doomsday trailer that you might have overlooked, so you can get fully up to speed on the Marvel Phase 6 movie.

So, for our deep dive, head to the below. Afterwards, be sure to check out our guide to all the upcoming Marvel movies for everything else that's on the way.

The main takeaway from the trailer is that Steve Rogers is well and truly back. He returns to action with Earth's Mightiest Heroes after a visit from the Fantastic Four. However, there's a lot to unpack here. For one thing, there appear to be two different timelines, identifiable by Steve having short hair in one, and longer hair and a bear in the other (plus, Peggy Carter goes from a vintage, period-appropriate look to a more modern style). It's also revealed that their son is much older than the baby we were introduced to in the first Doomsday teaser. If that wasn't enough, there's the question of what Loki visited Steve and Peggy for, if the Fantastic Four arrive to collect him later. Also, it's now clearer than ever that Steve going back to live with Peggy is indeed the catalyst for the film's plot.

Thor seems to give the assembled heroes in Avengers Tower a rousing speech that we hear just a snippet of. He urges them to put their differences aside, and he also acknowledges that he doesn't really know who everyone is. This feels like Marvel slyly poking fun at itself for the oversaturation of the past few years – and it also seems to be the "heroes finally stop bickering to come together" beat of the story.

The end of the trailer is enough to give even the most jaded of viewers chills. For the first time, we see the X-Men and the Avengers unite properly against Doctor Doom as the score blasts, in what looks to be the film's version of the "Avengers! Assemble" moment from Endgame.

Enough about the heroes: Doctor Doom doesn't feature heavily in the new trailer, but we do get an ominous glimpse of him flanked by his witchy backup. The VisionQuest post-credits scene revealed that one of these is none other than a freshly-resurrected Scarlet Witch, too.

We finally get to hear Cyclops say "to me, my X-Men!" in the fight at the X-Mansion. This is the first time the famous catchphrase has been said in the MCU by an X-Men member.

We know the plot will feature incursions, and in this trailer we see two worlds looking as if they're about to crash into Earth. Though, which worlds exactly are on the collision course remains to be seen.

The Avengers Tower has a fancy new entrance, which allows the Fantastic Four's ship to land inside the logo. Is this an upgrade that arrived after the Thunderbolts post-credits scene brought Marvel's First Family to the main timeline?

Tony Stark himself doesn't feature in the trailer, but his memorial does. The poignant Avengers: Endgame moment that saw his Arc Reactor floating in the water is shown again in the Doomsday trailer, when Steve is talking about the events of that movie. Considering we still don't know why Robert Downey Jr. is playing Doctor Doom, this feels like a significant tease.

We know the Avengers and X-Men will come to blows, but a split second moment in the final trailer shows Sam Wilson, AKA Captain America, and Cyclops fighting it out. Uh oh…

In another brief moment, we see Steve Rogers and Bucky Barnes joyfully embracing while Sam Wilson watches on, looking equally pleased. It's a nice reunion for the three best buds.

Bob, AKA Sentry, hasn't had a major presence in the marketing so far, but he can be seen sitting in the background of Avengers Tower.

Thor uses his yellow lightning powers in the trailer, which have been teased in posters so far. This could be the Odinforce, an incredibly strong power.

News of Kate Bishop's return broke ahead of the trailer, but we get our first look at her in the film in the new footage. It's a fleeting glimpse, however, and how she might be involved is anyone's guess.

We also get our first look at Ant-Man's daughter, Cassie Lang, in the new trailer. Like the Kate Bishop moment, it's very brief, but she doesn't look very happy.

Avengers: Doomsday arrives on December 16 in the UK and December 18 in the US. In the meantime, check out our guide on watching the Marvel movies in order to catch up with a marathon.

#3709. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was October's biggest game in the US, but it wasn't enough to crack 2026's best-selling top 10

Despite its somewhat muted critical reception, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has predictably topped the US video game charts in October. The Infinity Ward-developed shooter was October's best-selling game in the US across digital and retail, beating the month's other big-hitters, including Gears of War: E-Day and Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

That's according to market analysis firm Circana's latest US market report, which revealed Modern Warfare 4 was October's leader in dollar sales. This marks the 19th-year running that a Call of Duty game topped the charts in its release month, a streak that began with November 2008's COD: World at War.

However, despite a successful October, Modern Warfare 4 hasn't managed to land in Circana's top ten list of year-to-date biggest sellers. In fact, the only COD title on the list is the Black Ops 2 port released this summer. NBA 2K27 continues to lead Circana's ranking, having overtaken Resident Evil: Requiem last month to secure the top spot. It's a reverse of Circana's September report, when NBA 2K27 failed to lead its own debut month but claimed the top spot in the year-to-date list. Here's the list of the top 10 year-to-date:

Away from Modern Warfare 4, October saw the release of several other well-performing and critically acclaimed games, and six of the top ten were new releases. That hasn't stopped Circana from posting 14 percent lower spending on games compared to October last year. Analyst Mat Piscatella noted much of that dip can be attributed to a big slump in mobile spending, and also because October 2025 was particularly strong, with both Battlefield 6 and Pokémon Legends: Z-A releasing. Here's October's top 10:

In Eurogamer's Modern Warfare 4 review, Dom Peppiatt awarded it four stars, writing: "Modern Warfare 4 represents the highest tide for Call of Duty in seven years. Infinity Ward needed to pull off a balancing act I don't envy; injecting just enough nostalgia into a series propped up with so many conventions and expectations there's barely room for anything new, alongside enough innovation and intrigue to keep people interested."

#3708. Arknights: Endfield version update ‘Meeting You in the World o’Shrooms’ launches November 25

Publisher GRYPHLINE and developer Mountain Contour will release the version update “Meeting You in the World o’Shrooms” for free-to-play 3D RPG Arknights: Endfield on November 25, the companies announced. The game’s latest live stream also introduced the upcoming version 2.0 update, which takes players to Gypsosia and aboard the Rhodes Island landship, and teased 10 characters who will join the journey across upcoming content updates.

“With Wuling’s story wrapping up, and the main story taking us through all the heavy moments, we want to give you a change of pace with a lighthearted, upbeat update,” said Arknights: Endfield producer Light Zhong in a press release.

Here is an overview of the update, via GRYPHLINE:

Version Update “Meeting You in the World o’Shrooms”

Strange mushrooms have overrun an abandoned dam outside Wuling, where Landbreakers worship a giant mushroom and visitors keep slipping into hallucinations. There, the Endministrator meets Kay, a Rhodes Island Operator who has been adventuring alone across Talos-II in search of them. Kay happily shares everything she treasures, including a towering stack of honey waffles. But which would she choose: a mountain of waffles or a dear friend?

A Nature Vanguard with a carefree fighting style, Kay throws weapons that scatter across the battlefield, then gathers them up for a heavy hammer slam. Along the way, she drops Picnic Snacks that heal her teammates.

The Old Dam, the update’s new area, has grown into a fairytale-like mushroom kingdom. Players fire Kay’s honey waffles at mushrooms to open doors and spin fungal bridges, and must avoid Loquacious Shrooms that scramble their sense of direction. Mushroom foes like the Bolete Prince guard the dam, and a mushroom as tall as a mountain waits at its heart.

The update’s music leans into its whimsical tone, with Ori composer Gareth Coker and ambient producer Owsey returning to score Kay’s honey waffle adventure. It caps a first year in which the soundtrack has followed the story, from the sweeping sci-fi orchestral sound of Valley IV to the choir-driven battle against Alleikhreos, Typhoeus’s JRPG-inspired winter journey and the modern electronic take on Eastern music in Si’s painted world.

Later in the update, every player who logs in during the Workers’ Guards: Roll Call event will receive the Operator Mimino and her signature weapon, Star of Tomorrow, for free, with event missions offering extra copies to reach full Potential. Operators Gilberta and Rossi also return in successive reruns.

For factory builders, Exclusion Zone Rebuilding is a new permanent mode in which players supply materials across four phases to restore the North Wuling Exclusion Zone, using the new Forge of Luminance to transform products on their conveyor belts. For a lighter break, Lucky Carrot’s Games of Wonder adds two multiplayer card games, Witch’s Darkjack and Band Uprising, that players can enjoy with friends or through matchmaking.

A First Look at Version 2.0 and Rhodes Island

The livestream also previewed the next chapter of Arknights: Endfield, arriving in the new year. Exiles have launched attacks across the Civilization Band, and their real target is Rhodes Island. The Endministrator sets out with Perlica into Gypsosia, the Cretaceous Frontiers, where players will be able to board and explore Rhodes Island itself, a massive landship. A 10-character teaser offered a glimpse of companions for the journey, including Warfarin, appearing as the leader of Rhodes Island, and M3, who returns looking completely different.

The chapter’s first update will add four new maps at once, including Rhodes Island. Main Mission Early Unlock: Gypsosia will let players who have completed the main mission Remediation Progress skip ahead to the new story while still earning all beginner-event rewards. New modes are also in development for future updates, including a management sim with the Golden Branch Tribe and the Shattered Protocol combat mode.

Arknights: Endfield is now Steam Deck Verified, with default controller support and every feature available on Valve’s handheld. The update also brings Despot Weaponized, a new high-difficulty challenge series in Umbral Monument; the return of RISE! MEGA ARENA!, a two-Operator arena event; and new seasons of the Echoes of War combat mode.

Arknights: Endfield is available now for PlayStation 5, PC via the official launcher, Steam, and Epic Games Store, iOS via App Store, and Android via Google Play.

Making sure your animations don't break while you're cultivating mass.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We don't know precisely how big GTA 6's "big boy" budget was, but let's put aside the alarming excess of contemporary mass-consumption entertainment for a moment and talk about the real big boy: bulked up Jason.

While GTA 6's body morphing might not go quite as far (in terms of waistband measurements) as its predecessor San Andreas—or even a game like Fable 2—it does boast extensive variety of different body shapes among its cast, and making that work at such a high level of visual fidelity took an entire dedicated team.

In an interview with IGN, Rockstar vice president of animation Mark Tennant said it was an early decision in development to "push the variation in character sizes and body types … This required us to establish a very robust way to share animations between characters while still resolving multiple points of contact, such as most vehicle interactions and grappling in hand-to-hand combat."

It also took eschewing a "traditional approach" in favor of "new techniques," the sort I imagine you can only implement at Rockstar levels of budget and manpower. "We also had to grow a team dedicated to overseeing the implementation, which required close collaboration with the art and rigging teams," said Tennant. "All these aspects needed to come together to make it work, so it was a huge team effort."

In the same IGN piece, senior technical art director Valmor Garcia said the ultimate goal was to ensure each character had "singular awareness and visual identities," which included giving them unique faces and anatomy (the six-figure animation count is part of that too, I imagine). All the blood, sweat, and so on seem to be paying off given the game's absolutely massive launch, but Saints Row 3 is still the only crime sandbox that lets me replace all my character's dialog with meaningless zombie grunts, so it's impossible to say which is better.

#3706. Only two days out from GTA 6, its publisher Take-Two lay off staff at XCOM and Civilization developer Firaxis

About a third of the workforce has been cut, reportedly

Upsettingly, it is that time of the week again, as Take-Two are laying off staff at Firaxis, the developer behind Civilization and XCOM, only a little over a year the last time the studio suffered from layoffs. Firaxis are, notably, owned by Take-Two, the publisher of GTA 6 which comes out in, oh, two days time? Interesting timing, 'ey.

Word of the layoffs came from Bloomberg, who report that about 60 people are losing their jobs, apparently roughly a third of its staff. The studio's head, Heather Hazen, is also leaving. A spokesperson for 2K Games (the Take-Two label that manages Firaxis) shared a statement on the layoffs: "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years.

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis." I don't feel personally confident in the idea that the only way to make a company succeed is by laying a bunch of people off thereby making it much harder to make anything in the first place, especially in the lead-up to what will likely be the best selling game of the decade, but what do I know!

Bloomberg also report Firaxis have been working on a new XCOM, which is yet to be announced, but the project has apparently had to contend with numerous development issues, missing a "significant milestone over the summer." This new XCOM game hasn't been cancelled at the very least, but anonymous sources that spoke with Bloomberg said it may have to deal with a shakeup due to the cuts. As always, solidarity with all those affected by this situation.

#3705. Avengers: Doomsday final trailer has convinced me Steve Rogers got the bad ending in Endgame

This is what it's like when worlds collide

The Avengers: Doomsday final trailer is here, and it's all about Steve Rogers – from his personal sacrifice of leaving behind Peggy and their son, through to joining Thor and the OG X-Men in a battle against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom.

But the first minute or so of the trailer is riddled with inconsistencies about the one-time Captain America – and I think it's telling us more than it's letting on.

The opening seconds of the Doomsday trailer again shows the moment Steve and Peggy reunite in Endgame. Then, it has a montage of a clean-shaven Steve packing away his Captain America gear, holding his baby boy, and later teaching him how to ride a bike.

But the Steve we have seen so far – both in this trailer and elsewhere – shows him with longer hair and a beard, even right up to when the Fantastic Four rock up outside his doorstep.

Apart from telling us that Doomsday picks up with Steve and Peggy having a teenage son sometime in the early 1960s, it appears that the Fantastic Four aren't crossing the multiverse to meet him.

Instead, my theory is that Steve actually ended up visiting Peggy on Fantastic Four's Earth-828, a decision that caused much of the multiverse to collapse upon itself – and put Steve in Doom's sights.

"We didn't know those choices would have consequences," Steve Rogers says of the decision to travel through time in Avengers: Endgame to reclaim the Infinity Stones and use them against Thanos in the Battle for Earth.

Simply put, Steve Rogers' past and present actions are catching up to him. He shouldn't have gone back through time (on either occasion), he is potentially on the wrong Earth, and he has a son that should never have existed.

So, Avengers: Endgame's final dance could actually be the opening salvo to the universe ending – and caused the incursions (such as the worlds appearing in the sky in one Doomsday trailer moment) that is leading to the collapse of the universe. Good job, Steve.

Avengers: Doomsday hits cinemas on December 14 in the UK and December 16 in the US.

#3704. What would Rockstar have done if GTA hadn't taken off? Former tech director Obbe Vermeij on Scottish zombies, James Bond and the "curse" of success

"We ended up just cutting and cutting it."

It's bizarre today to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't Grand Theft Auto. Frankly, it's bizarre to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't GTA 6, which rolls onto console hard drives this week. A decade in the making, with a development team of thousands scattered across an international network of studios, GTA 6 aims to be the Maximum Game. It's both a dense, lively open world and a monument to the exhausting impersonality of "triple-A" game productions. It contains multitudes: birdlife! Realistic cloud formation! Fuel mechanics! Romance! Soda visibly sloshing around in bottles! It's an imperial production shadowed by labour disputes, that appears to have given Rockstar's various teams little time or space to think about anything else.

It wasn't ever thus. Once upon a time, Rockstar weren't just known for GTA and to a considerably lesser extent, Red Dead Redemption. Once upon a time, they had a reputation for slightly dodgy experiments. I recently interviewed former Rockstar North tech director Obbe Vermeij about a few of them, including Agent, the unofficial James Bond game Rockstar toyed with before putting all chips on Grand Theft Auto 5.

During the noughties especially, when the most expensive games took considerably less time to make, Rockstar tried their hand at a number of projects besides GTA. There was 2002's Manhunt, a rancid parody of snuff films – not much loved, but sufficiently admired to spawn a sequel in the hands of Rockstar London. There was 2005's adaptation of Walter Hill flick The Warriors - a mouthy Homeric beat 'em up in which you cross New York on foot over the course of a single night - and 2006's Rockstar Presents Table Tennis - an inexplicable pivot towards realistic sports simulation from Rockstar San Diego. Later in 2006 came Bully, aka Canis Canem Edit, a boarding school life sim from Rockstar Vancouver (née Barking Dog Studios). I didn't warm to Bully, myself, but I've never been able to get its sardonic OST out of my head.

In amongst all these, Rockstar weighed up several game projects that never made it out of the building. The aforesaid Agent is perhaps the best-known, but my conversation with Vermeij (who worked at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009) began with "Z", a fleeting attempt to expand into the world of zombie action games, which Rockstar spent a few weeks mulling over in the wake of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. It was set in the islands of Scotland, which would have made it the only Rockstar North project to unfold in the studio's backyard. "I think it was meant to be smaller than GTA, map-wise, and there weren't going to be any deserted cities - it was really just islands and some villages," Vermeij told me. "But it really didn't get that far."

The pitch for Z couldn't be further from the sweat and glitter of GTA 6's Miami, but the two projects would have shared a taste for 'simulation' elements. "It actually was going to have cars running out of fuel," Vermeij told me. "That was going to be one of the things, and the whole idea was that you'd find cars and they'd only have a little bit of fuel in them." As for why Z never entered full development, turns out desolate North Atlantic archipelagos full of corpses can be a bit of a downer. "Everybody was super excited to do something new," Vermeij went on. "And then pretty quickly, we kind of realised that it's really just a depressing version of GTA, and it sort of died."

The increasing success of Grand Theft Auto during these years was something of a "curse", Vermeij went on. It meant that a lot of Rockstar's ventures beyond GTA were eventually folded back into the series. "It's very difficult to have a studio and have one mega game, and then do something on the side," he explained. "It's almost impossible, because at any time during the development of the smaller project, management's going to say 'oh! The big project's in trouble. We need more people.' And they're just going to pull everybody from that small team onto the big team, so even if we had progressed with [Z], what would have happened is we would have had to start GTA 4 at the same time, and eventually the small team would just be merged with the big team again."

Rockstar's Bondalike game Agent got a lot further down the road to release than Z. It was in development for several years following GTA 4's launch, and was touted by co-founder Sam Houser as Rockstar's next megagame. "A lot of work had been done on that," Vermeij recalled. "And then we ended up just cutting and cutting it, because the same thing happened – at some point you kind of go OK, well, we better get on with the next GTA."

Agent sounds like it could have been a hoot, at least going by Vermeij's description of his own time with the project. It was a relatively linear, level-based action game with a touch of camp. "There was a French ski resort, and there was going to be a Mediterranean town like San Tropez, somewhere like that," Vermeij explained. "There was going to be a North African place, like Morocco or Egypt. The last level was going to be on the moon, with lasers – like Moonraker. There was another one, London or something, I can't remember. But then we just ended up cutting everything down, because what we could see happening was that at some point, we would have to go back to work on GTA. It wasn't close to being finished."

While never a spoof in the vein of Austin Powers, Agent would have been a sillier production than the grimy and downbeat GTA 4. "It was meant to lean into all the cliches," Vermeij said. "It was like James Bond from the 1970s - there was a girl with white boots. It wasn't a comedy, it was just completely over-the-top cliched."

As for the choice of a level-based format, this came from a desire for variety the studio couldn't realistically achieve in a GTA-style open world. "If you had to have them all on one map, you would basically have had to model a mini version of Europe," Vermeij said, "So you couldn't do that." Players might have been able to revisit locations containing several missions, which calls to mind Io Interactive's later Hitman: World of Assassination games, to say nothing of their own bash at the Flemingverse, 007 First Light. "I don't how whether it was going to be completely linear, or whether you were always going to be able to visit all those locations." Vermeij said.

Needless to say, Rockstar's Bondalike would have featured chase scenes. Vermeij himself worked on the moving parts. "I remember doing some work on what we called the car recording stuff for GTA," he went on. "So if a level designer wanted to set up a chase scene, they would drive one car, record it, and then play back the recording, drive a second car and record that... and so driving one by one, you could set up a whole chase scene. I did a version of that for [human] characters as well, because for one of the Agent missions in the French ski resort, there was like a chase where the bad guys were on skiis and using their machine guns. So I set up a thing where you'd play them one by one, and then play the whole thing back. There was maybe like five or six bad guys and they'd ski after you, and then it was just up to the player to avoid them."

According to Vermeij, Agent never had a defined story during his time with it. It was more of a mix of scenario concepts, "kind of how we used to do games with GTA 3 and Vice City". Mind you, the absence of a nailed-down plot isn't necessarily a sign that Agent was lightyears from being finished. Even at their most byzantine, Bond movie plotlines often feel like an afterthought. "It's like oh yeah, there's a bad guy and there's a thingally-dingally that needs to be captured before the world comes to an end," summarised Vermeij. Still, Agent would spend a long time in limbo after Vermeij left. It's still unclear how much it was in active development before Rockstar's trademark finally evaporated in November 2018.

One thing I learned while reading up on Rockstar's checkered history was that GTA 3, the game that made GTA a Thing on PlayStation, wasn't deemed an immediate hit at launch. According to Vermeij himself, it was months before Rockstar realised what they'd built. This inspired an obvious closing question: what might Rockstar have done, if GTA 3 hadn't blown up the way it did? Which of those other projects might have become the focus?

"I really have never thought about it," Vermeij pondered. "When Rockstar San Diego joined, it was 2002, and they already had a bunch of games and a bunch of franchises, like Midnight Club and Smuggler's Run. They were already into driving games and city games in that way, so it wouldn't have surprised me if we'd gone in that direction anyway. But then they were more about car modding and decals and stuff like that.

"At Rockstar North, we only had Manhunt and GTA," he went on. "With Manhunt, that team was in development hell for a while, they had a couple of rough years where they got stuck and in the end, they pulled through, and they got a pretty decent game. But I don't think that would have been the future. I don't think [Rockstar North] would have done a Manhunt 2. So yeah, it would be Table Tennis, I think! Everything on Table Tennis!"

#3702. As Rockstar's alleged "union busting" tribunal hearing comes to a close amid GTA 6 launch, judge pledges to deliver verdict "as quickly as I possibly can"

Closing statements in Rockstar and IWGB's employment tribunal case - revolving around the GTA 6 developer's alleged 'union busting' and the firing of 34 employees - have now been read, bringing the hearing to an end. There's currently no timeline for a verdict, however, with one commentator suggesting a judgement could take weeks or months to arrive.

The case, which began in September and has included evidence from 23 claimants in the months since, must now be considered by the judge, who will determine if Rockstar unfairly dismissed employees in breach of their employment rights. Rockstar has been accused of unlawfully firing workers for being part of a union, but the GTA developer insists employees were dismissed for breaching confidentiality agreements.

People Makes Games' Chris Bratt has been following the case closely and reporting on proceedings as they've unfolded. With closing statements now complete, Bratt quoted Judge Lucy Wiseman as saying, "I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case. What I will say is that I will use my best endeavors to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can."

However, Bratt suggests it could be ""anywhere from a few weeks up to a few months before we actually hear the judgement", noting "The firings themselves, let's not forget, happened over a year ago now. This has been a slog."

One fired Rockstar worker involved in the case spoke with Bratt after the closing statements to share their thoughts. "Honestly it's just sort of blended together," they said. "It’s been so long, that after the first six months or so it became the new depressing reality. I'm hoping the judgement will release us from it."

Last month, the conclusion of the tribunal hearing was delayed after cross examination of witnesses ran long.

Yesterday's closing statements come at a time when all eyes are on GTA 6 as it finally releases this week, concluding years of development for both current and former employees. Many of those workers involved in the case urged players to support the game despite the legal dispute.

Additionally, Rockstar employees are currently voting on whether they want recognised union representation at the studio. If the vote passes, it would be the largest recognised union across the entirety of the UK video game industry. The deadline for union votes is 26th November.

Unreal Engine 6 will not launch with the engine's long-standard Blueprints scripting system. The news came in a Friday, November 19 post on the Unreal Engine website, written by Epic Games executive vice president of development, Marcus Wassmer. Here's Wassmer's top-level summary from the post:

"UE6, including UE6 Early Access, won’t include Blueprints or the Actor Gameplay Framework. Gameplay will be built in Verse and on the new Scene Graph framework.

"In June, we said Blueprints and Actors would coexist in UE6 Early Access and 6.0, so UE5 projects could upgrade incrementally while the new Scene Graph framework matures. However, with recent advances in AI capability, we expect AI to massively help with converting UE5 projects to UE6, if not make that process fully automatic. That also means we can deliver UE6 on time (or sooner!) while meeting its design goals: a new data model, a Verse-first architecture, modularity, and AI operability."

Blueprints have not (and it appears, will not) be deprecated in Unreal Engine 5, and the company maintains that projects will still be easy to convert from UE5 to UE6. Wassmer cited a declining cost in AI task completion as one reason for this belief, as well as the team's ongoing, but apparently successful conversion of Fortnite's Blueprint library to UE6's Verse programming language through an AI-assisted process.

Blueprints are a widely-used feature of Unreal. Former Valve developer Chet Faliszek, an AI skeptic, has put out a vlog on the subject. Essentially, Faliszek argues that Blueprints (and features like them in other game engines) represent a middle ground between artistic and technical work, an introduction and skill builder for less technically-minded developers. Without them, such developers seemingly have to either learn Verse code, or integrate LLM prompting into their workflows.

"We made a new skill in the middle there, between normal and expert," Faliszek said of intermediate tools like Blueprints. "To lose that determinism from game design, and instead have to prompt AI⁠—or write your own Verse … It's losing those tools that made all those designers and all those artists so powerful, to be able to do really powerful things and have access to really deep-down things, but in a safe way that the engineers can decide what that meant to them."

A dark horse game of the year candidate, the first-person RPG Queen's Domain, was made with Unreal Engine. I recently spoke to co-developer Eric Berger, who specialized in art and design alongside the more technically-focused Bradley Boothe, a relationship that rhymes with the ones Faliszek outlined in his video.

I spoke to Berger before seeing Epic's latest press release, but Berger already indicated that Unreal's AI pivot is prompting Freshly Baked Games to switch engines for its next project. I followed up with Berger about this Blueprint news, and the developer said that Blueprints were a major part of the workflow on Queen's Domain.

I'm a layman in game development, but I think Wassmer's post elides that there is a large qualitative difference between doing any work via LLM prompt versus the old-fashioned way⁠—I don't like or want to use these tools, myself, and I don't think that's an unpopular stance. Commenter ZILtoid1991 on Faliszek's video compared the move to Apple removing headphone jacks on the iPhone, a comparison I find fruitful.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

It was hugely unpopular at the time, and is still derided by enthusiasts, but it also worked. Other manufacturers copied Apple, and everybody has bluetooth headphones now⁠—or Apple's own, proprietary Air Pods. But Apple had far less success trying something similar with its laptops: The lack of ports on late 2010s Macbooks proved disastrous, and Apple has since reintroduced more (and a wider variety of) ports on newer models of the popular line. I certainly have my own anti-AI, pro-headphone jack preferences, but we'll have to see how this plays out with the Unreal Engine.

#3700. Warren Spector lambasts GTA 6's "billion dollar" development - 'I just hope it's is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer'

"A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries."

As GTA 6 finally arrives, increasingly outspoken games industry legend Warren Spector - known for seminal immersive sims including Deus Ex - has offered both praise for the game's achievements and lambasted its "billion dollar" development model, writing, "I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it’s the best we have to offer".

Spector announced his retirement from games development in August following struggles at his OtherSide Entertainment studio, and has been vocal about the state of the games industry in the months since, notably saying anyone at EA responsible for the "travesty" of BioWare's closure should be "ashamed". And now Spector has taken on GTA 6.

"First, congratulations to everyone who worked on GTA 6. It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," he wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "However… its billion dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate.

"That's especially true," Spector continued, "when thousands of developers are out of work. A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries. Personally I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is."

The "sure success" of GTA 6 proves a point he's made "for years", he said: "That no game that matters ships on time and/or on budget". Highlighting GTA 6's year-long delay and reported billion dollar budget, Spector suggested, "Give a game the time and money to prove its potential (key word, potential) and you have a chance of making something great. Underfund a game or force it out the door before it's ready [is] guaranteed failure no matter how much potential it has.

"So, again, congratulations," Spector concluded. "Ambition and innovation are necessary for the medium to reach its potential. I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer."

Despite Spector's concerns, GTA 6's arrival is, as expected, already causing shockwaves across the industry. It has broken pre-order records for Xbox and PlayStation stores, smashed the all-time livestream viewer record, and apparently briefly broke Reddit too. And is its success deserved? Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell thinks so, saying it "pushes back the horizon of video games once again" in his five star GTA 6 review.

#3699. Archetype go all in on the Mass Effect vibes with a FemJun reveal, but I'm just left hoping they'll call the alternative option MascJun to balance it out

I know it, you know it, hell, I'm sure developer Archetype Entertainment know it: Exodus is kind of just Mass Effect again. That's in part because the DNA of the game has been built by series vets like Drew Karpyshyn, Chad Robertson and James Ohlen. But it's also because, well, they're putting FemShep in the game. Yes, I'm being a tad facetious here, but when the latest trailer for your game is literally titled "Female Jun Reveal," well, comparisons will be made!

To top it all off, a blog post from the devs literally refers to the alternate gender for the protag as FemJun. They know what they're doing. In any case, first up, her voice actor! She's being played by Carina Conti, an up and comer last digitally heard in Mafia: The Old Country as Isabella Torrisi. Male Jun (who hasn't been given a nickname, which couldn't possibly serve to other female Jun (and MascJun is right there!)) has also had his voice actor confirmed as Stephen Oyoung, who you'll have heard as Mister Negative in Insomniac's Spider-Man games and Red Hood in Gotham Knights.

It's been previously confirmed that no matter which gender you pick for Jun, you'll be able to romance whoever you like, so, happy smoochin'! The story will stay the same too, as will dialogue options, though I'm imagine some pronoun switcheroos will take place somewhere along the line.

I'm mostly just left feeling that this doesn't really seem like it'll fix the game's boring hero problem. Edwin made note of Jun's quite lacklustre vibe earlier this year, aptly tearing down MascJun's Instagram visage, though this was prior to the face model and voice actor change the character has undergone. Personally, I'm not sure that'll be enough, and FemJun kind of matches that Instagram look; the perfect bun and bangs that pop out when she takes her helmet off is quite silly too. Ah well! A game isn't done until it's done (which, in theory, will be April 7th next year).
